books.title: Frogs and Toads
books.art_why: Real frogs, toads, and their habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: I Found a Frog! Have you ever seen an unusual animal in nature? Did you want to learn more about it? Last week I saw a really neat frog, and that was the start of a wonderful adventure. What does a frog say when it sees something great? Toadly awesome!
pages.brief: A curious child stands outdoors in a grassy natural area, looking closely at a frog near the ground. The child leans in with interest, clearly excited by the unusual animal. The frog sits calmly among grass and low plants, and the child watches it as the start of an adventure.

pages.text: I looked for the frog in a a field guide. I started pictures in the book. I was see all the of frogs and toads. It Do You Know? I saw a wood frog.
pages.brief: The child sits with a field guide open, turning through pages filled with pictures of frogs and toads. The child pauses to look at a wood frog shown among the pictures. The field guide rests open as the child studies the many kinds of frogs and toads.

pages.text: I wanted to know more, so I went to the Internet. Did you know that frogs and toads are relatives of newts and salamanders? They’re all they live part of their life in water and part on land. Amphibians are animals. They don’t make their own body heat. They get warmth from the heat of the sun.
pages.brief: The child sits at a computer, looking at a screen with images of frogs, toads, newts, and salamanders. The scene shows these amphibians both in water and on land. Sunlight shines down, suggesting the warmth amphibians get from the sun.

pages.text: Life Cycle I also learned that most frogs and toads lay jelly-covered eggs in water. The babies that hatch are called tadpoles and look like little fish. Tadpoles breathe with gills, just like fish, and they live in water. But it’s amazing what happens as they grow!
pages.brief: In shallow water, clusters of jelly-covered frog and toad eggs rest together. Nearby, tiny tadpoles that look like little fish swim with small tails. The tadpoles stay underwater, breathing with gills as they grow in their watery habitat.

pages.text: Their gills disappear, and they grow lungs so they can breathe air like other land animals. They grow legs and then arms. Later, their tail shrinks. By the time their tail is gone, they move onto land. I saw some very cool photos of the life cycle of frogs and toads.
pages.brief: A series of close views shows a tadpole changing: its gills disappear, lungs develop, legs and then arms grow, and its tail shrinks. At the end, a young frog moves onto land. The child looks at these cool photos of the life cycle of frogs and toads.

pages.text: About Frogs Frogs are famous for their ability to leap with their long, strong back legs. They leap to catch insects and other prey. A frog can catch an insect in an instant with its long, sticky tongue. Why are frogs so good at baseball? Because they catch a lot of flies.
pages.brief: A frog leaps through the air with its long, strong back legs stretched out. Ahead, an insect flies near the frog. The frog's long, sticky tongue reaches out to catch the insect in an instant, showing how frogs leap to catch prey.

pages.text: The eyes and nostrils of a frog are on the top of its head. Frogs can see, smell, and breathe while they’re mostly under water. In fact, they breathe through their skin while they’re under water! Frogs can make an of noise. Male frogs sing loudly to attract a mate. Do You Know? What has more lives than a cat? A frog—it croaks every night.
pages.brief: A frog floats mostly underwater, with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface. It can see, smell, and breathe while hidden in the water. Nearby, a male frog sings loudly with its mouth open, making noise to attract a mate.

pages.text: Do you know the differences between frogs and toads? Here’s what I learned from a book at the library. Frogs Toads.
pages.brief: At the library, the child sits with an open book about frogs and toads. On the pages, a frog and a toad are shown side by side so their differences can be compared. The child studies the two animals carefully, learning what makes frogs and toads different.

pages.text: Defense I was sad to learn that frogs and toads are food for many other animals. Bats, snakes, birds, and rodents all hunt them. But frogs and toads have clever ways to stay What happens when frogs park illegally? might try to They get toad away. eat them.
pages.brief: A bat, a snake, a bird, and a rodent are near frogs and toads in a natural setting. The frogs and toads are food for these hunters, so they need clever ways to stay safe. The predators search around them while the frogs and toads remain alert.

pages.text: Some frogs and toads, like the wood frog I saw, are the same color as their habitat. This is called blending in. It allows them to hide better from predators. Some kinds of frogs are so poisonous that just touching their skin is deadly. These frogs are brightly colored to warn predators to stay away. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A wood frog sits on ground that matches its own color, blending in with its habitat. Because it hides so well, it is harder for predators to spot. Elsewhere, a brightly colored poisonous frog stands out clearly, warning predators to stay away.

pages.text: Some frogs try to trick predators that might want to eat them. The tomato frog puffs up like a balloon when a snake gets near. The snake thinks the frog is too big to eat. If the snake tries to eat it anyway, the frog leaks a liquid like glue from its skin.
pages.brief: A tomato frog puffs up large like a balloon as a snake comes near. The snake looks at the swollen frog, which seems too big to eat. If the snake tries anyway, the frog can leak a glue-like liquid from its skin.

pages.text: Why are frogs so happy? They eat whatever bugs them. Frogs Are Cool! Frogs and toads come in many shapes, sizes, and colors. You can find them in trees, in or near water, and on the ground. One thing is true about all of them—they’re amazing animals. What kinds of frogs have you seen?
pages.brief: Frogs and toads of many shapes, sizes, and colors appear together. Some sit in trees, some are in or near water, and others rest on the ground. The scene shows how amazing these animals are and invites the viewer to think about frogs they have seen.

books.title: You Stink!
books.art_why: Real skunks, other animals, and habitats exist today.

pages.text: Nobody Likes You! Imagine that you are a four-legged animal about the size of a cat. You have short legs and a long, bushy tail. Your soft black fur has long white stripes. You are a beautiful animal, but nobody wants to be your friend. Why not? You’re a skunk, and you stink! Anyone who smells you or gets sprayed by you never forgets it.
pages.brief: A striped skunk stands alone outdoors, shown from the side so its short legs, long bushy tail, and soft black fur with long white stripes are clear. It is about the size of a cat. The skunk looks calm and beautiful, with no other animal nearby.

pages.text: You and your smelly cousins live in many parts of North and South America. Striped skunks—your kind—are the skunks most people know about. Hooded skunks look like you, but more of their fur is white. Hog-nosed skunks look like hooded skunks with long noses. Spotted skunks have white spots or short stripes. Do You Know?
pages.brief: Several kinds of skunks are shown in natural habitats across North and South America: a striped skunk with black fur and white stripes, a hooded skunk with more white fur, a hog-nosed skunk with a long nose, and a spotted skunk with white spots and short stripes.

pages.text: What Kind of Animal? You are a mammal. This large group also includes whales, bears, deer, mice, and many other animals. Like other mammals, you have a backbone and hair, and your babies are born live. The mammals on this page are some of your closest relatives.
pages.brief: A skunk is shown beside other mammals: a whale, a bear, a deer, and a mouse. The animals appear together to show the large mammal group. The skunk has a backbone and hair, and its babies are born live, like the other mammals pictured.

pages.text: Like many of your relatives, you like to eat both animals and plants. More than half of your food is insects. You also like to eat worms, frogs, rodents, lizards, snakes, birds, and eggs. Some of your favorite plants are grass, leaves, nuts, and berries. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A skunk searches for food outdoors among low plants. It eats both animals and plants: insects, worms, frogs, rodents, lizards, snakes, birds, and eggs, along with grass, leaves, nuts, and berries. More than half of its food is insects.

pages.text: Why You Stink You have a secret weapon to keep enemies away. You only use it after you try everything else. First, you feet if an close. Then you hiss and growl. If your tail and arch your back. You try to look bigger to scare the enemy.
pages.brief: A skunk faces an enemy and gives warning signs. It stamps its feet, hisses, and growls. Then it raises its tail and arches its back, trying to look bigger to scare the enemy away near its outdoor home.

pages.text: Sometimes these warnings do not work. Then you spray your enemy with a sticky, smelly Do You liquid called musk. Know? Musk comes from a pouch at the bottom of your tail. Musk smells worse than terrible. It takes a long time for the strong smell to go away.
pages.brief: A skunk turns its back toward an enemy and sprays sticky, smelly musk from a pouch at the bottom of its tail. A smelly spray comes from the skunk. The skunk stands outdoors, using its secret weapon after its warnings did not work.

pages.text: What animals are enemies of you and your stinky cousins? Most other mammals leave you alone. Your black-and-white fur is a warning to keep away. But some large animals think of you as a tasty meal. Great horned owls are your worst enemy. They have a very poor sense of smell.
pages.brief: A great horned owl swoops near a skunk outdoors. The skunk’s black-and-white fur stands out as a warning to keep away. Most mammals leave the skunk alone, but the owl has a very poor sense of smell and sees the skunk as a tasty meal.

pages.text: Skunk Homes Your home is called a den. You might make your home inside a hollow log. Many of your cousins live in underground burrows. If you live you may live under a house. You are careful not to home. You animals do!
pages.brief: A skunk enters a den inside a hollow log. Nearby, other skunks are in underground burrows, and one skunk is under a house. The den is the skunk’s home, and the animals are careful around their homes.

pages.text: You spend winter in your den, but you don’t sleep all winter as bears do. On warmer come out to look for food. You don’t other skunks. But on cold Do You Know? many of you in a den to keep warm.
pages.brief: In winter, a skunk stays in its den but is awake, not sleeping all winter like a bear. On a warmer day it comes out to look for food. In cold weather, many skunks gather together in a den to keep warm.

pages.text: Baby Skunks If you are a female skunk, you give birth to babies in the spring. The babies are called kits. You usually have five or six kits at one time. Your kits are born with skin that is black and white. Their skin has the same pattern of color that their fur will have someday.
pages.brief: A female skunk rests in a den with five or six newborn kits in spring. The babies have black-and-white skin with the same color pattern their fur will have. The mother skunk stays close to her tiny kits.

pages.text: You stay in your den with your kits for about six weeks. Like other mammals, you feed your babies milk so they will grow. Then you take your kits outside. You protect them from animals that might want to eat them. Your kits learn how to find food and stay safe. After nearly a year, they leave you to live alone.
pages.brief: A mother skunk stays in the den with her kits for about six weeks, feeding them milk. Then she takes the kits outside and protects them from animals that might eat them. The kits learn to find food and stay safe before leaving after nearly a year.

pages.text: Skunks and People You and your smelly cousins want people to leave you alone. If people come too close, you might spray them. You might try to bite or scratch, too. Some of your cousins have a sickness called rabies. Rabies can kill people. This is another good reason for people to leave you alone. But the biggest reason is because you stink! Do You Know?
pages.brief: A skunk stands outdoors near people and gives a warning. If people come too close, the skunk might spray, bite, or scratch. Some skunks have rabies, which can kill people. The biggest reason people should leave skunks alone is the terrible stink.

books.title: How Much Is a Trillion?
books.art_why: Real-world photos suit the book’s concrete comparisons: cities, people, pennies, buses, and football fields.

pages.text: Really Big Numbers What’s the biggest number you can think of? One hundred? One thousand? Ten thousand? We use special words such as and trillion to talk about numbers. But what do these words mean? And what do a million, a billion, and a trillion look like?
pages.brief: Three vast groups of tiny objects stretch across an open landscape, each group far larger than the one before, suggesting a million, a billion, and a trillion; the smallest group is already huge, and the scene feels wide and imaginative.

pages.text: Hide and Seek Have you ever played the game of hide and seek? In hide and seek, one person counts up to a number while everyone else hides. But some numbers are so big that you couldn’t count up to them in your whole lifetime.
pages.brief: In a leafy backyard on a sunny afternoon, one child stands with hands over eyes, counting while several other children scatter to hide behind trees, bushes, and a small shed; the scene is playful and suspenseful.

pages.text: How Much Is a Million? We write one million as a one followed by six zeros, like this: 1,000,000. Do you know how much a million is? Some of the world’s largest cities have millions of people living in them. If you are lucky, you might win a million dollars in a lottery. Ten Largest Cities in the World.
pages.brief: A sprawling city skyline packed with apartment towers and busy streets suggests millions of people, while in the foreground a hand holds a shining lottery ticket beside a wide jar of coins; the mood is hopeful and bustling.

pages.text: I’ve Told You a Million Times! Maybe you think your parents have told you to clean your room a million times. But have they really? Let’s say that every day your parents tell you ten times to clean your room. You would be over 273 years old before they told you for the millionth time!
pages.brief: A parent stands in a messy bedroom, gently urging a child to tidy toys and clothes, while a small calendar and many rows of tiny blocks suggest repeated reminders; the child looks resigned, surrounded by clutter.

pages.text: A Million Pennies Imagine a jar with one thousand pennies in it. Now imagine one thousand jars, each with one thousand pennies inside. That’s a million pennies.
pages.brief: A single clear jar sits in the foreground filled with many pennies, while behind it rows and rows of identical penny-filled jars fill the room and stretch into the distance, creating an overwhelming sense of one thousand jars.

pages.text: Ready or Not, Here I Come! Remember our earlier game of hide and seek? Let’s say you count to one million while your friends run and hide. You will count for over three weeks without stopping before you reach one million. Your friends will probably be very well hidden by then.
pages.brief: Children play hide and seek outdoors; one child stands counting at a tree with a patient expression, while other children hide far away in bushes, behind benches, and near a playground, looking settled in for a long wait.

pages.text: How Much Is a Billion? We write one billion as a one followed by nine zeros, like this: 1,000,000,000. There are more than seven billion people alive on Earth right now. More than one billion of them are under the age of ten years old. That’s a lot of kids!
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth from space shows glowing clusters of city lights across continents, suggesting billions of people, while a bright band of many children’s faces circles the globe to represent over one billion kids under ten.

pages.text: But how much is a billion? Imagine I gave you a million dollars every day. At that rate, it would take almost two years and nine months before you had one billion dollars.
pages.brief: A person stands beside a huge pile of dollar bundles that grows each day, with a long row of calendar pages stretching past almost two years and nine months; the person looks amazed at the towering total.

pages.text: How long do you think it would take to count to a billion during a game of hide and seek? If you counted that high, your game would last about one hundred years! And that’s if you didn’t stop to sleep, eat, drink, or do anything else while you counted.
pages.brief: A child stands alone counting in a quiet yard, while nearby trees grow tall and seasons change around the same spot; distant friends remain hidden, and an old, weathered look suggests a game lasting about one hundred years without stopping.

pages.text: A Billion Pennies Remember the jar of one thousand pennies? Imagine stacking one billion pennies up in the shape of a block. The block would be about the size of five school buses.
pages.brief: A colossal block made entirely of stacked pennies rests on a wide paved area, and five yellow school buses are parked alongside it to show the block’s enormous size; the penny block towers over the buses in a bright, open lot.

pages.text: How Much Is a Trillion? A billion is a big number, but a trillion is much larger. One thousand times larger to be exact. We write one trillion as a one followed by twelve zeros, like this: 1,000,000,000,000. But what does a trillion look like? Imagine that you stacked up one trillion pennies in the shape of a cube. Each side of the cube would be almost as long as a football field.
pages.brief: An immense cube built from countless pennies stands on a football field, with each side almost as long as the field itself; the cube dominates the stadium, dwarfing goalposts and sidelines, and the sheer scale feels almost impossible.

pages.text: Big Numbers Are Useful People who work in science, business, and government often use big numbers in their work. A scientist might use big numbers to measure the distance from Earth to the Sun. A businessperson might use them to count how many products a company has sold. A city planner might use them to decide how many schools a city with millions of people needs.
pages.brief: A scientist measures the distance from Earth to the Sun with instruments, a businessperson tallies stacks of products in a warehouse, and a city planner studies a model of neighborhoods with schools; all three work with large numbers in their jobs.

pages.text: Conclusion Knowing about millions, billions, and trillions can help us understand our world and our universe. So don’t be afraid of really big numbers and the words we use for them. Big numbers have a million uses!
pages.brief: A child gazes up at a starry night sky above a quiet neighborhood, with a sense of wonder about the vast universe; nearby everyday objects and distant stars suggest millions, billions, and trillions of possibilities.

books.title: Hermit Crabs
books.art_why: Hermit crabs and their beach and ocean habitats exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Shell-Changing Night A hermit crab hurries across the beach. An empty shell just washed in. The shell is a little bigger than the one he’s been using. He grabs the new shell with his claws. Then he pokes his head inside. It’s empty. He stands on two legs. Then he slips his body out of his old shell and into the new one. He’s in!
pages.brief: On a sandy beach at night, a hermit crab hurries toward an empty seashell that has just washed in. He grips the larger shell with his claws, pokes his head inside, stands on two legs, then slips out of his old shell and into the new one.

pages.text: What Do Hermit Crabs Look Like? Hermit crabs are related to other crabs and also to lobsters and shrimp. A hermit crab has its own hard outer shell, called an exoskeleton. But the exoskeleton only covers part of its body. A hermit crab wears an old seashell to protect its soft parts.
pages.brief: A hermit crab wearing an old seashell is shown with its hard exoskeleton covering only part of its body; nearby a crab, a lobster and a shrimp show its relatives. The old seashell protects its soft parts.

pages.text: A hermit crab has five pairs of legs. The first pair of legs ends in claws. The second and third pairs are for walking. The fourth and fifth pairs are short. The crab uses the little back legs to hold onto its shell home. A hermit crab also has two pairs of antennae. They help the crab taste water and find food. There are more than eight hundred different kinds of hermit crabs. Some are as tiny as a penny. Others are as big as a softball.
pages.brief: A close-up of a hermit crab beside its shell home shows five pairs of legs: claws in front, walking legs next, and short back legs gripping the shell. Two pairs of antennae extend forward. A penny and a softball suggest the smallest and largest kinds.

pages.text: How Do Hermit Crabs Live? Hermit crabs live in warm oceans all around the world. Some hermit crabs live on beaches or in tidal pools. Others live in the water. All hermit crabs are scavengers. They will eat just about any food they can find. Seaweed? Love it. Dead fish? They’re great. Rotting wood? Dinner is served.
pages.brief: In a warm ocean and a tidal pool, hermit crabs search for food. One walks on a beach, another rests in shallow water. Nearby are seaweed, a dead fish and rotting wood, foods these scavengers will eat.

pages.text: Hermit crabs are mostly nocturnal, which means they move around at night. They hide in their shells during the day. Baby Hermit Crabs Hermit crabs start as eggs. The eggs hatch in the water, and larvae (LAR-vee) float out. The larvae look like tiny shrimp. For a few months, they grow and change shape. When they are big enough, they find an empty seashell and join the colony.
pages.brief: During the day, a hermit crab hides inside its shell; at night another moves across the sand. In the water, eggs hatch and tiny shrimp-like larvae float. A young crab finds an empty seashell and joins a colony.

pages.text: As young hermit crabs grow, their exoskeletons don’t get any bigger. So every year or so, they molt. They get rid of their old exoskeleton and grow a new one that’s the right size. Hermit crabs can live to be thirty years old, but most live six to ten years. Danger! Birds, octopuses, fish, and other animals will eat hermit crabs if they can. If a crab senses danger, it pulls into its shell and sits still.
pages.brief: On sand, a hermit crab has climbed out of its old exoskeleton and grown a new one. Nearby, a bird, a fish and an octopus threaten it. The crab pulls into its shell and sits still, hidden from danger.

pages.text: Not Really Hermits Hermit crabs got their name by mistake. Hermit crabs hide inside their shell “homes” when they are scared. People thought this meant they wanted to live alone, like hermits. But these crabs don’t like to live alone at all. They like to live in groups. Hermit Crabs: Not Easy Pets Many pet stores sell hermit crabs. But hermit crabs can be tricky to care for. The crabs need a moist area. They need to be calm. They need places to dig. And they need other crabs. Hermit crabs that don’t get the right care suffer and sometimes die. If you want to keep hermit crabs as pets, please learn to give them what they need to be healthy and happy.
pages.brief: Several hermit crabs gather on sand, not living alone like hermits. One hides inside its shell. In a pet-store habitat, a crab has a moist area and places to dig, with other crabs nearby for company.

pages.text: Watch Them Run! Hermit crabs look funny when they run across the sand. But they do more than make us smile. Hermit crabs have important jobs to do. They keep beaches clean by eating dead fish and plants. Seeing hermit crabs is usually a sign that a beach is healthy.
pages.brief: Several hermit crabs run quickly across the sand, looking funny as they move. One eats a dead fish and another eats a plant, helping keep the beach clean. The busy crabs and clean sand show a healthy beach.

books.title: Parrots
books.art_why: Real parrots, scientists, and habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: A male eclectus parrot in Singapore uses its beak to clean its tail feathers.
pages.brief: A male eclectus parrot in Singapore perches among tropical foliage and bends its head to run its beak along its tail feathers. Its bright green body, wings, and long tail are clearly visible as it cleans itself.

pages.text: Two sun parakeets share a meal of leaves. There are many interesting birds in the world, and parrots are among the most amazing. What makes parrots so special?
pages.brief: Two sun parakeets, bright orange and yellow, perch close together and share a meal of green leaves. Their beaks touch the leaves as they feed, and their long tails hang down against a leafy background.

pages.text: Parrots come in many sizes, shapes, and colors. Many parrots are beautiful, with bright feathers in one or more bold colors. Parrots can be green, blue, yellow, red, or a mix of many colors. They can also be black, white, or gray. They can even be pink! Parrots.
pages.brief: Several parrots of different sizes and shapes perch together, showing bright feathers in green, blue, yellow, red, black, white, gray, and pink. Some birds display one bold color, while others show a mix of many colors.

pages.text: Dr. Irene Pepperberg studied the intelligence and communication skills of African grey parrots, such as Alex (shown here), for many years. Parrots are super smart. Like humans, apes, and dolphins, parrots’ brains make up a big part of their bodies. Large brains give parrots the ability to learn, remember, and. Scientists have studied some parrots that are as smart as children in kindergarten.
pages.brief: Dr. Irene Pepperberg works with Alex, an African grey parrot, studying the bird’s intelligence and communication skills. Alex perches close by while she observes him, showing one of the parrots scientists have studied for many years.

pages.text: What parrots are best known for, however, is their ability to learn and sounds. Many parrots can repeat words or sounds they hear. Some parrots can even speak using hundreds of different words. African grey parrots are famous for their speaking ability. Some African greys can tell jokes, count, and correctly name shapes and colors. Some of them can even speak in more than one language! Know? Humans use vocal cords to talk, but parrots don’t have vocal cords. Parrots have to change the shape of the walls of their throats to speak. Parrots.
pages.brief: An African grey parrot perches in a bright setting, its beak open as it repeats words and sounds. The bird represents parrots that can learn hundreds of words, tell jokes, count, name shapes and colors, and speak more than one language.

pages.text: True parrots, cockatoos, and New Zealand parrots look very different. What Makes a Parrot a Parrot? There are more than 350 different kinds of parrots. The three main groups of parrots are true parrots, cockatoos, and New Zealand parrots. Although parrots come in many different shapes and sizes, they are all alike in some ways. What’s in a Name? Parrots include many different birds, such as: Amazon parrots, African parrots, macaws, parakeets (including budgerigars or “budgies”), parrotlets, conures, lories, lorikeets, lovebirds, cockatoos, cockatiels, kakas, kakapos, and keas.
pages.brief: Three parrots stand together to show the main groups: a true parrot, a cockatoo, and a New Zealand parrot. Their shapes and sizes differ, with the cockatoo’s crest visible, while the others show different body forms and feather patterns.

pages.text: Almost all parrots have large, with a pointed upper half and a short, strong lower half. Parrots are sometimes called because their upper bills are shaped like hooks. Strong bills allow many parrots to crack open nuts and fruits that other animals can’t. Parrots also use their bills to hold objects, clean their feathers, and help them climb. Parrots use their large, strong beaks to help them in many ways. Parrots.
pages.brief: A close view of a parrot’s large, strong bill shows a pointed upper half and a short, strong lower half shaped like a hook. The parrot uses the bill to crack open nuts and fruits, hold objects, clean its feathers, and help itself climb.

pages.text: Parrots’ unusual feet allow them to do things other birds can’t. All parrots have four toes on each foot, with two toes pointing forward and two pointing backward. They use their feet for climbing, cleaning their heads and beaks, and grabbing and holding objects. They are the only birds that hold their food in one foot while they eat it. Do You Know? Because they have toes pointing both forward and backward, parrots are good at hanging upside down. Some parrots, known as hanging parrots, even sleep upside down!
pages.brief: A parrot grips a branch with its unusual feet, two toes pointing forward and two pointing backward. It holds food in one foot while eating and can hang upside down. The image shows how these feet help with climbing, cleaning, and grabbing objects.

pages.text: Parrots have large, round heads with eyes on the sides. Most have circles of skin around their eyes where there are no feathers. Some parrots have a, or crown, of feathers on the top of their heads. Cockatiels and cockatoos can raise and lower the feathers on their crests. They use their crests to with other birds and to scare away predators. The bare patch of skin around A Major Mitchell’s cockatoo raises a parrot’s eye its crest. Parrots.
pages.brief: A Major Mitchell’s cockatoo raises its crest of feathers on top of its head. The bird’s large, round head shows eyes on the sides and a bare patch of skin around the eye. The raised crest is used to communicate and scare away predators.

pages.text: A macaw eats palm fruit The brush-tipped tongue of a lori in Ecuador. allows it to gather nectar. What Parrots Eat Parrots eat fruits, nuts, seeds, flowers, and other plant parts. Some also eat insects and other small creatures. A few kinds of parrots feed on nectar, a sugary liquid made by flowering plants. These parrots have special tongues that help them get nectar from flowers. Wowser! Parrots live a long time. Some larger parrots can live to be more than 85 years old!
pages.brief: A macaw grips and eats palm fruit in Ecuador. Nearby, a lori extends its brush-tipped tongue to gather nectar from a flower. The two birds show parrots eating fruits, plant parts, and sugary nectar using their special bills and tongues.

pages.text: An Amazon parrot makes its home in a rainforest in Peru. Where Parrots Live Most parrots live in warm in tropical and subtropical areas. Central America, South America, and the islands in and around Australia have the greatest variety of parrots. NORTH EUROPE AMERICA ASIA Subtropics AFRICA Tropics SOUTH AMERICA Subtropics AUSTRALIA Parrot range Parrots.
pages.brief: An Amazon parrot perches in a rainforest in Peru, making its home among warm tropical trees. A world map shows the parrot range across Central America, South America, Australia, and nearby islands, with tropical and subtropical areas marked.

pages.text: A blue-fronted parrot perches in a tree hollow in Brazil. Only a few kinds of parrots build nests. Most parrots live in hollow spaces that grow naturally in tree trunks. Some dig holes in cliffs, banks, or the ground. Do You Know? A parrot’s beak never stops growing. The beak is made of hard keratin, a much stronger version of what your fingernails are made of. Parrots need to eat hard, solid foods often to wear down their beaks so they don’t grow too large.
pages.brief: A blue-fronted parrot perches at the entrance of a tree hollow in Brazil. The hollow is a natural space in the trunk, showing where many parrots live instead of building nests. The bird’s strong beak is visible as it grips the wood.

pages.text: Parrots Are Popular Parrots are the rock stars of the bird world. Their beauty, intelligence, and playfulness have made them popular with people everywhere. Parrots As Pets Many people keep parrots as pets. Unfortunately, parrots can be hard to care for properly. Because they are very smart, parrots get bored easily, so they need a lot of attention. books.title: History of the Bicycle
books.art_why: The book covers 1800s inventions and early bicycles, when photographs of these events were impossible or rare.

pages.text: Introduction People started building bicycles in the 1800s. Since then, bicycles have grown more and more popular. Today, more than one billion people around the world ride bicycles. The design of bicycles has changed over time. However, they still have two wheels and are a lot of fun!
pages.brief: Show people in the 1800s building early bicycles, then a wide modern scene of more than one billion riders around the world enjoying bicycles today. Include bikes with two wheels, showing how the design changed over time but stayed fun.

pages.text: Early Bicycles Karl Drais built the first bicycle in 1817. He called his invention the running machine. The frame and wheels were made of wood. It had no pedals. Instead, the rider pushed the bike along with their feet.
pages.brief: Show Karl Drais in 1817 with the first bicycle, called the running machine. Its frame and wheels are made of wood, and it has no pedals. Show the rider pushing the bike along with their feet on the ground.

pages.text: After that, inventors made many changes to the bicycle. Around 1840, the first pedals were added. The pedals turned the rear wheel with cranks. These were attached to long rods. Pedals kept the rider’s feet off the ground.
pages.brief: Show inventors around 1840 adding the first pedals to a bicycle. The pedals turn the rear wheel with cranks attached to long rods. Show a rider using the pedals, keeping their feet off the ground.

pages.text: During the 1860s, two French inventors made pedals that turned the front wheel. Their new bike had a heavy iron frame. Its tires were made of iron or wood.
pages.brief: Show two French inventors in the 1860s with their new bicycle. Its pedals turn the front wheel, moving the bike forward. The bike has a heavy iron frame, and its tires are made of iron or wood.

pages.text: The Ordinary Built in 1871, the ordinary had a tall wheel in front and a small wheel in back. The rider sat on a seat above the front wheel.
pages.brief: Show the ordinary bicycle built in 1871. It has a tall wheel in front and a small wheel in back. Show the rider sitting on a seat above the front wheel, making the ordinary clearly different from earlier bicycles.

pages.text: The ordinary moved faster than earlier bikes because of its large wheel. The big wheel also caused problems. It was hard to ride up a hill. It was also hard to get on and off the high seat. Riders often fell onto their heads when they tried to slow or stop the bike. These problems made this bike dangerous.
pages.brief: Show an ordinary bicycle moving faster than earlier bikes because of its large wheel. Show a rider struggling to ride up a hill and to get on and off the high seat. Show the rider falling onto their head while trying to slow or stop.

pages.text: The Safety Bicycle John Starley created the Rover safety bicycle in 1885. It looked like the bicycles of today. Most safety bicycles moved on two wheels of about the same size. A low seat between the wheels made the bike safer and easier to ride. The first safety bicycles had solid rubber tires. Later, these were changed to air-filled rubber tires. They made for a much less bumpy ride!
pages.brief: Show John Starley with the Rover safety bicycle he created in 1885. It looks like bicycles of today, with two wheels of about the same size and a low seat between them. Show solid rubber tires, then air-filled rubber tires for a less bumpy ride.

pages.text: The safety bicycle used a gear and chain system. A chain connected gears on the back wheel to another gear. That gear was attached to the pedals. Riders pushed the pedals to turn the back wheel. Gears of different sizes made it easier to ride uphill, downhill, or on flat roads. Safety bicycles were less dangerous and more comfortable than earlier bikes. Because of this, more people began riding bicycles.
pages.brief: Show the safety bicycle’s gear and chain system. A chain connects gears on the back wheel to another gear attached to the pedals. Show a rider pushing the pedals to turn the back wheel, with gears of different sizes for uphill, downhill, and flat roads.

pages.text: The Golden Age of the Bicycle In 1885, there were hundreds of bicycle factories in the United States. By 1900, over ten million people in the country owned bikes. Bicycles improved and became more popular. In 1889 Isaac Johnson, a Black American inventor, created a folding bicycle. In the 1890s, a Roadster bike was invented for women. This made it easy for women to get onto and ride their bicycles. It often came with a skirt guard. This stopped skirts and dresses from tangling in the rear wheel. These years became known as the Golden Age of the Bicycle. The Golden Age ended in the early 1900s. That is when factories started to produce inexpensive cars.
pages.brief: Show hundreds of bicycle factories in the United States in 1885 and over ten million owners by 1900. Show Isaac Johnson, a Black American inventor, with his folding bicycle in 1889. Show a woman on a 1890s Roadster with a skirt guard, and early 1900s cars ending the Golden Age.

pages.text: The Future of Bikes Today’s bikes have the same basic form as the safety bicycle. However, the design has changed many times. New materials make bikes stronger, faster, and lighter.
pages.brief: Show today’s bikes with the same basic form as the safety bicycle. Show a modern bicycle beside the basic safety bicycle shape, and show the design changing many times. New materials make bikes stronger, faster, and lighter.

pages.text: The Bicycle: A Time Line On a recumbent bicycle, the rider sits low and leans back. These bicycles began appearing in the early 1900s. They are popular with riders today for their comfort and speed.
pages.brief: Show a recumbent bicycle with the rider sitting low and leaning back. These bicycles began appearing in the early 1900s. Show the rider in a comfortable position, and show that recumbent bicycles are popular with riders today for their comfort and speed.

pages.text: Every year, people invent new ideas for bicycles. One inventor has designed a bike to ride over land and water. People make bicycles out of recycled materials like plastic, wood, and bamboo. Bikes will continue to change. Who knows what bikes of the future will look like?
pages.brief: Show an inventor with a bicycle designed to ride over land and water. Show bicycles made out of recycled materials like plastic, wood, and bamboo. Show people inventing new ideas for bicycles every year, with future bikes still unknown.

books.title: The Story of Rapa Nui
books.art_why: The book covers ancient moai creation and 1800s events before photographs could show them.

pages.text: Island of Mystery Deep in the South Pacific is a place called Rapa Nui. It is also known as Easter Island. The island is home to about six thousand people and hundreds of giant stone statues called moai. It is also home to many stories and legends.
pages.brief: A wide view of Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island, deep in the South Pacific. About six thousand people live among hundreds of giant stone statues called moai. The island community and its many stories and legends surround the statues and homes.

pages.text: Who Made the Moai? About nine hundred years ago, Polynesian people came to Rapa Nui. The island is very hard to get to. The nearest land is over a thousand miles away. The people made Rapa Nui their home and named a king. They are believed to have made the moai.
pages.brief: Polynesian people arrive at Rapa Nui about nine hundred years ago, settling on an island over a thousand miles from the nearest land. They make the island their home, name a king, and are shown with the moai they are believed to have made.

pages.text: Why Were the Moai Made? The 887 moai might have been made as symbols of power and religion. They might also have been made to remind people of their ancestors. Many moai are found near fresh drinking water. They are also found near places where people probably grew gardens. So, they might have been created to mark fresh water.
pages.brief: Hundreds of moai stand as symbols of power and religion and as reminders of ancestors. Many are near fresh drinking water and near places where people probably grew gardens. The statues may have been created to mark that fresh water.

pages.text: Walking Statues? Scientists found a pit where the moai were cut from a stone wall. They also discovered the stone tools used to make the moai. However, scientists were still not sure how people moved the moai to the edge of the island.
pages.brief: Scientists stand in a pit where the moai were cut from a stone wall. They have found the stone tools used to make the moai. They still look uncertain about how people moved the statues to the edge of the island.

pages.text: Many moai are the size of two tall people. They are as heavy as a school bus. They are too heavy to drag around. The people of the island had no carts.
pages.brief: Many moai are as tall as two tall people and as heavy as a school bus. The statues are too heavy to drag around, and the people of the island had no carts to move them.

pages.text: Scientists wondered if tree trunks were used to roll the moai. But the Rapa Nui people living on the island today have stories and songs about walking statues. Could they be true?
pages.brief: Scientists wonder whether tree trunks were used to roll the moai. Rapa Nui people living on the island today tell stories and sing songs about walking statues, raising the question of whether those tales could be true.

pages.text: A Rapa Nui scientist said yes! So, another group of scientists did some tests to see if moai could walk. They tied long ropes to the top of a moai. People pulled on the ropes. The statue rocked back and forth. The moai moved forward little by little as the people pulled. The moai was walking!
pages.brief: A Rapa Nui scientist says yes, so another group of scientists ties long ropes to the top of a moai. People pull the ropes. The statue rocks back and forth and moves forward little by little. The moai is walking.

pages.text: The Mysterious Past Some parts of the history of Rapa Nui are still mysterious. There may once have been as many as 10,000 people on the island. By 1877, only 111 people were left. There are different ideas about when people disappeared—and why.
pages.brief: A once-busy Rapa Nui with as many as ten thousand people is contrasted with a nearly empty island where only 111 people are left by 1877. Different ideas about when people disappeared and why remain part of the mysterious past.

pages.text: One idea was that as people cut down the island’s many trees, the soil needed to grow crops washed away. This could have caused people to starve. Rats, which came to the island on the Rapa Nui people’s boats, also ate many nuts from the trees. This would cause fewer trees to grow. However, now scientists know the Rapa Nui people also had successful gardens. The trees were gone, but the people could still eat food from gardens.
pages.brief: People cut down the island’s many trees, and soil needed for crops washes away, which could cause starvation. Rats arrive on boats and eat nuts from trees, so fewer trees grow. Later, successful gardens still feed the Rapa Nui people after the trees are gone.

pages.text: Some people disappeared because they were enslaved. In 1859, people came from Peru to Rapa Nui. They enslaved about 1,500 people from the island and took them away. People from other countries also brought sicknesses that caused people on Rapa Nui to die.
pages.brief: People from Peru come to Rapa Nui in 1859 and enslave about 1,500 islanders, taking them away. People from other countries also bring sicknesses that cause people on Rapa Nui to die, leaving the island diminished.

pages.text: A year later, in 1860, island stories say that a civil war took place on Rapa Nui. Two groups, the Long-Ears and the Short-Ears, fought. Weapons discovered later by scientists support this story. Around the time of the war, some moai were pushed over. No one is sure why. Some think the moai were tipped face down to protest the war.
pages.brief: Island stories say a civil war takes place in 1860 between two groups, the Long-Ears and the Short-Ears. Weapons later found by scientists support the story. Around that time some moai are pushed over, and some think they were tipped face down to protest the war.

pages.text: Rapa Nui Today Thousands of Rapa Nui people live on the island and in Chile today. Some of them study the moai. In 1989, Rapa Nui scientists discovered pieces of shells that turned out to be moai eyes. As time goes on, people will continue to discover more about the amazing moai and the people who created them.
pages.brief: Thousands of Rapa Nui people live on the island and in Chile today. Some study the moai. In 1989 Rapa Nui scientists discover pieces of shells that turn out to be moai eyes. People continue to discover more about the amazing moai and the people who created them.

books.title: Empire State Building
books.art_why: The Empire State Building is a real place that exists today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Two Friends Think Big Two friends, John Raskob and Al Smith, wanted to build the tallest skyscraper in the world. They grew up in low-income families. Both had to quit school and go to work. Years later, Raskob was rich and Smith was famous. Together, the two friends made a good team and built the Empire State Building. Their building was the tallest in the world for forty-one years.
pages.brief: John Raskob and Al Smith appear as two friends planning the tallest skyscraper in the world, with a glimpse of their low-income childhoods and leaving school to work, and later Raskob rich and Smith famous beside the Empire State Building they built, tallest for forty-one years.

pages.text: Stars and States Take an elevator to the top of this building, and you can see parts of five states. Look around and you might see stars, even in the daytime. Famous movie stars visit to see the view, too.
pages.brief: A visitor rides an elevator to the top of the building and looks out over parts of five states; stars twinkle in the daytime sky, and famous movie stars visit the same view from high above New York.

pages.text: Making Room for Greatness The place Raskob and Smith chose for their building was a busy one. A grand hotel was already standing there. The hotel had to go. People worked day and night to tear down the hotel quickly. The two friends needed to construct their building fast.
pages.brief: The busy New York site chosen by Raskob and Smith, with a grand hotel already standing there, and workers tearing the hotel down day and night so the two friends can construct their building quickly.

pages.text: A skyscraper as big and heavy as the one they planned needed to sit on solid rock. Workers dug down 40 feet (12.2 m) to reach solid rock. Huge trucks carried away tons of dirt and rock. It took five months to tear down the hotel and make the hole. Then, on April 7, 1930, construction of the Empire State Building began.
pages.brief: Workers dig down forty feet to solid rock while huge trucks carry away tons of dirt and rock, after five months of tearing down the hotel and making the hole, with construction of the Empire State Building beginning on April 7, 1930.

pages.text: Sky Boys Strong metal beams rose. Beams support the skyscraper much as your bones support your body. As the steel beams went higher and higher, crowds gathered on the streets below. They looked up in wonder as men walked the narrow beams high above. People called the men “sky boys.”
pages.brief: Strong metal beams rise high above the street as the skyscraper grows in New York, while men walk along narrow steel beams and crowds gather below looking up in wonder at the workers called sky boys.

pages.text: Do You Know? Sky boys worked in teams of four to join the beams together with red-hot rivets. Every team member was brave and fast. The steel beams zoomed up an amazing four floors a week. Some of the best teams were the Mohawk from New York State. Some of them could set a rivet every minute.
pages.brief: A team of four sky boys works high on the steel beams, joining them with red-hot rivets, brave and fast, while the beams rise four floors a week and Mohawk workers from New York State set rivets every minute.

pages.text: Zoom to the Top By June, the steel reached the 25th floor. Behind the sky boys came other workers. They built the outside wall of the building. These workers were so fast that they started to catch up to the sky boys.
pages.brief: By June the steel beams reach the twenty-fifth floor; behind the sky boys, other workers build the outside wall of the building, moving so fast they start to catch up to the sky boys high above the street.

pages.text: August was the busiest month. The sky boys were almost to the top. The outside wall made of stone, windows, and metal was going up a floor a day. Inside, thousands of workers were busy.
pages.brief: In August, the busiest month, the sky boys near the top of the skyscraper while the outside wall of stone, windows, and metal rises a floor a day, and thousands of workers are busy inside the building.

pages.text: Getting supplies to so many workers was taking too much time. Workers laid tracks around each floor to speed things up. Carts were loaded and pushed along the tracks right to the workers.
pages.brief: Workers lay tracks around each floor inside the rising skyscraper to speed up supplies, with carts loaded and pushed along the tracks right to the many busy workers so they do not lose any time.

pages.text: In November, Al Smith stood proud. He was on the 102nd floor. The steel beams had reached the very top. He was also scared standing that high up on a beam. The last rivet was placed. When he smashed it into the beam, the steel work was done! That rivet made newspaper headlines. Not only was it the last one set, but it was also the only one made of gold.
pages.brief: In November, Al Smith stands proud and scared on the 102nd floor as the steel beams reach the very top; he smashes the last rivet, made of gold, into the beam, completing the steel work and making newspaper headlines.

pages.text: Happy Birthday! The building opened on May 1, 1931. Fifty years later, in 1981, the building was made a landmark. It is protected by law and cannot be torn down. Al Smith said his building was made for the future, and he was right! It will be standing tall in New York for a long time to come.
pages.brief: The Empire State Building opens on May 1, 1931, and fifty years later in 1981 becomes a protected landmark by law; Al Smith's building stands tall in New York, made for the future and unable to be torn down.

books.title: Incredible Places to Stay
books.art_why: The hotels, animals, and places are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: 2 6 3 7 4 Introduction Get ready to go on a tour of some of the world’s most amazing hotels. You’ll swim to the bottom of the sea, sleep in a cave, and meet different animals. Pack your bags and let’s go!
pages.brief: A child zips up a packed travel bag, ready to begin a tour of the world's most amazing hotels. The bag is full, and the child looks excited to set off on the journey ahead.

pages.text: Sky High The first stop on your tour is Skylodge Adventure Suites in the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. You can sleep and eat in see-through capsules hanging high above the valley floor. Each capsule is solar powered and has a view of Sacred Valley. You’ll feel just like you’re in a giant bird nest!
pages.brief: See-through capsules hang high above the valley floor of the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. Inside one capsule, a bed and a small table show where guests sleep and eat. A guest gazes out at the valley. Each capsule has a solar panel.

pages.text: A Cool Place to Stay The next stop on your tour is the Hôtel de Glace (O-tel DEH GLAHS) located outside of Quebec City, Canada. How cool is it? It’s a work of art made of ice! The rooms, halls, and most of the furniture are carved out of ice. It all melts away in the warm weather. Artists and workers spend about forty days every winter building it.
pages.brief: Outside Quebec City, Canada, the Hôtel de Glace glows white and blue. Inside, halls and rooms are carved from ice, with ice furniture. Artists and workers shape blocks of ice with tools, building the hotel in winter.

pages.text: You’ll need to wear your heavy winter clothes during your stay. It’s as cold as a freezer in there! You’ll sleep in a special sleeping bag because the beds are made out of ice.
pages.brief: A guest in heavy winter clothes stands in an ice room at the Hôtel de Glace. The bed is carved from ice, and a thick special sleeping bag lies on top. Frosty air fills the room.

pages.text: Breakfast with Giraffes From Canada, you’ll travel to Giraffe Manor in Kenya. The forests around the hotel are home to some of the tallest giraffes in the world.
pages.brief: Giraffe Manor stands among green trees in Kenya, with tall giraffes wandering in the forest around the hotel. The long-necked animals reach up to browse leaves near the building, and the hotel building peeks through the trees.

pages.text: Every morning, the giraffes leave the forest for the hotel. They stick their heads through open windows and doors. Guests feed breakfast to the giraffes. Profits made by the hotel support endangered animals.
pages.brief: At Giraffe Manor in Kenya, a giraffe stretches its long neck through an open window. A guest holds out food at breakfast time. Another giraffe stands by an open door, and the hotel supports endangered animals.

pages.text: In the Trees The next stop on your tour is Sweden. There you’ll find the Treehotel: a hotel made up of strange tree houses. Six tree-house rooms hang 14 to 20 feet (4 to 6 m) off the ground. One room, the Mirrorcube, is covered with glass. This tree house blends in with the woods.
pages.brief: In a Swedish forest, six tree-house rooms hang 14 to 20 feet above the ground among the trunks. One room, the Mirrorcube, is covered in glass and reflects the woods around it, blending in with the trees.

pages.text: Branches around the Bird’s Nest tree house make it look like the home of a giant bird. Another tree house looks like a UFO from outer space.
pages.brief: In Sweden, a tree house called the Bird's Nest sits among branches woven around it, looking like a giant bird's home. Nearby, another tree house shaped like a UFO from outer space rests among the trees.

pages.text: A Room Without a View While you’re in Sweden, it is only a short drive to the deepest hotel room in the world. The Sala Silvermine Hotel sits on top of an old silver mine. Most of the rooms in the hotel are near the mine’s opening. You can also spend a night hundreds of feet underground in the Mine Suite. It is located more than 500 feet (152 m) beneath the surface. Dress in warm clothes. The temperature in the mine is only about 28°F (–2°C). However, the room is warmed to 64°F (18°C).
pages.brief: The Sala Silvermine Hotel sits above an old silver mine in Sweden. Most rooms are near the mine's opening, while the Mine Suite lies more than 500 feet underground. A guest in warm clothes stands in the chilly mine, where the room is warmed to 64°F.

pages.text: Sleeping with Fish The last stop on your tour is Jules’ Undersea Lodge in the Florida Keys. Be prepared to get wet! The lodge is 21 feet (6 m) underwater. You’ll need scuba gear to get to your room. Scuba Time.
pages.brief: Jules' Undersea Lodge sits 21 feet underwater in the Florida Keys. A diver in scuba gear swims down toward the lodge's room, surrounded by blue water and fish. Sunlight filters down through the surface above.

pages.text: For dinner, you can even order pizza. Someone from the hotel will swim it down to you in a watertight box!
pages.brief: A hotel worker in scuba gear swims down to the undersea lodge carrying a watertight box. Inside the box is a pizza ordered for dinner. The worker delivers it to a guest waiting in the underwater room.

pages.text: Conclusion From the forests of Kenya to the bottom of the sea, amazing hotels are everywhere. These incredible places to stay offer you far more than just a bed for the night. They offer you an experience that you’ll never forget! Polar Bear Fun.
pages.brief: A wide scene shows giraffes beside a forest hotel in Kenya and a small lodge on the seafloor, with amazing hotels found around the world. The scene celebrates places that offer far more than a bed and an unforgettable experience.

books.art_why: Ocean animals and real places are shown, so photographs fit.

pages.brief: A wide ocean scene filled with many different ocean animals swimming in blue water, while a few animals rest at the edge of a rocky shore. The water is busy with life, showing that some animals stay in the sea all the time and others spend time on land.

pages.text: As a dolphin, my sleek body and strong tail help me swim fast. I live with other dolphins in a group called a pod. We whistle, click, and squeak to talk to each other. I swim to the surface a few times a minute to breathe. My brain is large, so people think I’m pretty smart. I like to eat fish.

books.title: Endangered Birds
books.art_why: The book includes extinct and historical bird scenes best shown with drawings.

pages.text: Introduction Have you ever seen a great auk (AWK)? These penguin-like birds once lived along the coasts from Iceland to Florida. But the great auk was fiercely hunted for its feathers and eggs. The very last ones were killed in 1844. Today, great auks are extinct. You can only see them in pictures, or see their skeletons in a museum.
pages.brief: A great auk, a penguin-like bird with a black back and white front, stands on a rocky northern coast near Iceland and Florida, where these birds once lived. Nearby, feathers and eggs lie on the rocks, hinting at hunting. In a museum case, a great auk skeleton and an old picture show the extinct bird.

pages.text: There are many other birds that are endangered, or close to becoming extinct. We will look at some of those birds in this book. We will also see some ways that humans are trying to save them.
pages.brief: Several different endangered birds are shown in a wide natural landscape: some perched in trees, some flying over water, and some standing on grass. In the distance, people work carefully in the birds' habitats, showing that humans are trying to save these rare birds from extinction.

pages.text: The Kakapo The kakapo (ka-ku-po) of New Zealand is one of the strangest, and rarest, birds in the world. It has short wings and cannot fly, but it has strong legs to walk through the mountains. It looks like an owl, and it comes out at night like an owl. But the parrot. Male a booming call like a giant heartbeat.
pages.brief: At night in the mountains of New Zealand, a kakapo walks on strong legs. The owl-like parrot has short wings and cannot fly. A male kakapo stands nearby with its chest puffed out, making a deep booming call like a giant heartbeat that rolls across the dark mountain slope.

pages.text: Before Europeans came to New Zealand, there were few predators, or meat-eating animals, on the islands. Europeans brought cats, rats, and dogs to New Zealand. The kakapos had never seen these animals, so they didn’t know how to defend themselves. And they couldn’t fly to escape. The predators killed so many birds that by the 1950s, the kakapo disappeared.
pages.brief: On a New Zealand island, a kakapo stands on the ground while a cat, a rat, and a dog approach through the brush. The flightless bird has never seen these predators and cannot fly away. The animals surround the kakapo, showing how predators killed so many birds.

pages.text: Then, in 1974, a few males were found. But because there were no females to lay eggs, kakapos would become extinct once the males died. In 1980, four females were found. Humans moved the kakapos to small islands without predators. Scientists began breeding the kakapos, or helping them reproduce. Today, there are 62 kakapos.
pages.brief: Conservation workers carry kakapos onto a small island without predators. Scientists check the birds and help them breed. A few male and female kakapos are shown together on the island, while a worker watches over them, representing the small group that survives today.

pages.text: The Short-Tailed Albatross There were once millions of short- tailed albatrosses. These beautiful gull-like birds spend many years at sea before nesting. All the short-tailed albatrosses nested on a few islands around Japan.
pages.brief: Many short-tailed albatrosses, gull-like seabirds, glide over the ocean near a few small islands around Japan. Some fly far out at sea, while others gather above the islands where all short-tailed albatrosses once nested.

pages.text: About one hundred years ago, women loved to wear feathers in their hats. Hunters killed thousands of albatrosses for their feathers. Soon, there were none left on the islands. It seemed that the short-tailed albatross was extinct.
pages.brief: About one hundred years ago, women wear hats decorated with feathers. On islands, hunters gather albatross feathers and kill thousands of the birds. Soon the nesting islands are empty, with no short-tailed albatrosses left, making it seem the species is extinct.

pages.text: Years after the last albatross was seen, a few were spotted nesting on a volcanic island. These albatrosses had been at sea while the others were killed. They were the last short-tailed albatrosses alive. Today, the albatrosses’ island is protected. The birds are still in danger, though. The volcanic island might erupt, killing the last short-tailed albatrosses.
pages.brief: A few short-tailed albatrosses nest on the slopes of a volcanic island. Smoke rises from the volcano above them. These birds were at sea while others were killed, and they are the last alive. The birds nest on protected island slopes, but the volcano still threatens them.

pages.text: The California Condor The California condor is the largest flying bird in North America. For many years, farmers, ranchers, and hunters shot and poisoned these birds. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A California condor, the largest flying bird in North America, spreads its huge wings above ranchland. Below, farmers, ranchers, and hunters stand near fields. Some hold guns or poison, showing how these people once shot and poisoned the condors.

pages.text: In the 1980s, the last 27 living condors were caught. Now scientists take condor eggs and keep them warm until they hatch. Then, they hand-feed the chicks using condor puppets. The puppets help the chicks learn to live with instead of with humans. Once the chicks can fly, they are the wild.
pages.brief: In a warm nursery, scientists keep condor eggs warm until they hatch. A scientist hand-feeds a fluffy condor chick using a condor puppet. The puppet helps the chick learn to live with condors instead of humans. Once the chick can fly, it is released into the wild.

pages.text: The condors are still in danger after they are released. Some are shot. Others die by hitting power lines. Scientists still keep condors in zoos and raise chicks by hand. Someday all the condors may fly free.
pages.brief: A released California condor flies free above a power line, while another condor is kept in a zoo enclosure where scientists raise chicks by hand. The flying condor is still in danger: it may be shot or hit the power lines. Scientists hope all condors will someday fly free.

pages.text: Conclusion There are many other endangered birds in the world. Most are dying out because of human activity. But people are now trying to save these rare and beautiful animals from extinction.
pages.brief: Many different endangered birds are shown across a wide landscape: some flying, some perched on branches, and some standing on the ground. People below carefully watch over the birds and their natural places, showing humans trying to save rare and beautiful birds from extinction after much harm from human activity.

books.title: Art Around Us
books.art_why: The book shows real art forms and working artists that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Art is all around us. Art is in every shape, size, and color. Artists can make art from anything. Some artists make art with paint or paper. Others use glass or clay. Some use a computer. Others make art out of plants or sand.
pages.brief: A group of artists make art in different ways: one uses paint and paper, one works with glass and clay, one uses a computer, and another uses plants and sand. Their art appears in many shapes, sizes, and colors around them.

pages.text: Painter Some artists are painters. Most painters use a brush. Others like to splash or spray paint. Some like to drip paint instead. It’s all painting.
pages.brief: Several painters work at easels and on large surfaces. One painter uses a brush, another splashes paint, one sprays paint, and one lets paint drip. All of them are painting in their own way on their surfaces.

pages.text: Painters paint on many surfaces. Most paint on canvas. Some paint on dishes or furniture. Have you seen a painted mural? A mural is big. It’s painted right on a wall.
pages.brief: Painters paint on many surfaces. One works on canvas, one paints dishes, and one paints furniture. A painter makes a big mural right on a wall, and several people stop to look up at it.

pages.text: Sculptor Sculptors carve shapes with sharp tools. They might carve wood, stone, or ice. Other artists make soft sculpture. Soft sculptures are shapes made from fabric and yarn.
pages.brief: Sculptors carve shapes with sharp tools in different materials. One carves wood, one carves stone, and one carves ice. Other artists make soft sculptures from fabric and yarn, shaping the soft materials into forms by hand.

pages.text: Some sculptors shape metal. They pour hot metal into a mold and let it cool. When they take the sculpture out, it’s shaped like the mold.
pages.brief: A sculptor pours hot metal into a mold, then lets it cool. When the cooled metal sculpture is taken out, it has the shape of the mold. The sculptor works carefully with the hot metal.

pages.text: Potter Potters make art with clay. They use their hands to shape the clay. Potters push on the clay. They pinch it. They pull it. They make it into the shape they want.
pages.brief: A potter shapes clay with both hands. The potter pushes the clay, pinches it, and pulls it, working it into the shape they want. The clay sits on a work surface as the potter shapes it.

pages.text: The clay shape is baked in a very hot oven. The heat bakes the clay until it’s dry. Baked clay is called ceramic. Potters use a special ceramic paint called a glaze. The glaze makes the ceramic shiny.
pages.brief: A clay shape is baked in a very hot oven until it is dry. The baked clay is ceramic. A potter paints the ceramic with a special glaze, and the glaze makes the finished ceramic shiny.

pages.text: Glassblower Melted glass is soft, like very thick glue. A glassblower scoops up a blob of hot, soft glass with the end of a long metal pipe. The pipe is hollow, like a straw. The artist blows air through the pipe into the blob of glass. The air makes a bubble in the glass. Then the glassblower can shape the bubble. He or she can make it wide, like a bowl, or make it flat, like a plate.
pages.brief: A glassblower scoops a blob of hot, soft glass with the end of a long metal pipe. The hollow pipe works like a straw. The glassblower blows air through it into the glass, making a bubble, then shapes the bubble into a wide bowl or flat plate.

pages.text: Glassblowers work very quickly. While the glass is soft, they can change it. They can add dots or color. They can add a handle. But they have to be careful. When glass cools, it gets hard, and it can break easily.
pages.brief: A glassblower works quickly while the glass is soft. The artist adds dots, color, or a handle to the glass. The glassblower must be careful, because when glass cools it gets hard and can break easily.

pages.text: Fiber Artist Art can be made with thread, yarn, and pieces of fabric. It’s called fiber art. Some fiber artists sew. Some make a quilt for a bed.
pages.brief: Fiber artists use thread, yarn, and pieces of fabric to make art. Some fiber artists sew with thread. One fiber artist makes a quilt for a bed, joining pieces of fabric together into a quilt design.

pages.text: Weavers are also fiber artists. Weavers loop yarns together to make art. They use a machine called a loom. The loom helps them put the yarns in the right place. Weavers can make beautiful rugs or blankets. They can weave a soft sculpture to hang on a wall.
pages.brief: A weaver loops yarns together on a machine called a loom. The loom helps place the yarns correctly. The weaver makes a beautiful rug or blanket, and can also weave a soft sculpture to hang on a wall.

pages.text: Unusual Art Some art just looks different to us. It isn’t a painting. It isn’t a glass bowl. It’s hard to say what it is. Artists make it from found. Maybe they use pieces of wood and old junk. They might use parts of old toys, too. Some with sand. They get to work at the beach all day!
pages.brief: Some art looks very different: it is not a painting or a glass bowl, and it is hard to say what it is. Artists make unusual art from pieces of wood, old junk, old toy parts, and sand. Some artists work at the beach all day.

pages.text: Many artists like to work outside. They make art in a park or a garden. They use tree branches, rocks, and plants to make a design. People can come to the park to see it.
pages.brief: Artists work outside in a park or a garden. They use tree branches, rocks, and plants to make a design. People come to the park to see the outdoor art among the trees and plants.

pages.text: An art installation is big. It can be a whole room that is a work of art. Sometimes, you can walk around inside it. The artist fills the room with things to look at, touch, and hear. The room might have flashing lights or big video screens. You might hear music or strange sounds. You might smell flowers or popcorn.
pages.brief: A big art installation fills a whole room and is a work of art. A visitor can walk around inside it. The room has flashing lights, big video screens, music or strange sounds, and smells of flowers or popcorn.

pages.text: Where Art Is Found Simple drawings are the oldest art in the world. Some very old drawings are on the walls of caves. Other old drawings were scratched into rocks. The drawings tell stories about something that had happened long ago. Art is also found in the ruins of very old cities. Scientists sometimes find old pottery designs. Some ruins have old murals painted on the walls.
pages.brief: The oldest art in the world is simple drawings on cave walls and drawings scratched into rocks. These old drawings tell stories about things that happened long ago. In ruins of very old cities, scientists find old pottery designs and old murals painted on walls.

pages.text: Art is everywhere. Explore your town to find types of art. Visit an art museum. You will see many types of painting and sculpture. Go to an art gallery or an art fair. Artists want you to see and enjoy what they make.
pages.brief: Art is everywhere. People explore a town to find different types of art. At an art museum, an art gallery, or an art fair, visitors see many kinds of paintings and sculptures made by artists.

pages.text: Look for art around you. You can look for art when you are riding in a car. You might see a sculpture in a park. You might see a big mural on a wall.
pages.brief: A person riding in a car looks out for art around them. They might see a sculpture in a park or a big mural on a wall. Art can be found while traveling through town.

pages.text: You can make your own art. Draw on a sidewalk with chalk. Make a sculpture with clay, snow, or sand. Glue pieces of seashells, glass, and wood on a picture frame. It’s all art!
pages.brief: A child draws on a sidewalk with chalk. Another makes a sculpture with clay, snow, or sand. Someone glues seashells, glass, and wood onto a picture frame. Each person makes their own art from different materials.

pages.text: You can tell a story with art. It can help you say how you feel. Art can be interesting or funny. It can be something that you just like to look at. Look for art. You’ll find it all around you!
pages.brief: Art can tell a story and help someone say how they feel. Some art is interesting, some is funny, and some is just nice to look at. A person looks for art and finds it all around them.
