pages.brief: A collection of rectangular prisms is shown for readers to look at. The rectangular prisms vary in size and position. Each one has flat faces, straight edges and vertices. Some are close together and some are apart.

pages.text: Cubes A cube is another type of solid that is also a rectangular prism. It has six faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges.
pages.brief: A cube is shown as a solid with six faces. It has eight vertices and twelve edges. The cube is also a rectangular prism. Its six faces are equal squares, and its edges are equal all around.

pages.text: Look at the orange face on the cube. It is a square. The blue and yellow faces are also squares. All six faces are squares with equal edges all around.
pages.brief: A cube is shown with an orange face, a blue face and a yellow face visible. Each visible face is a square. All six faces of the cube are squares, with equal edges all around.

pages.text: Tanya looks for cubes in the toy store. She knows they have: • six square faces • eight vertices • twelve equal edges.
pages.brief: Tanya searches a toy store for cubes. Cubes are shown with six square faces, eight vertices and twelve equal edges. Tanya looks at the cubes among the toys in the toy store. The cubes are solid figures.

pages.text: How many cubes can you see?
pages.brief: A group of cubes is shown for readers to look at. The cubes are different sizes and placed in different positions. Each cube has square faces, straight edges and vertices. Some cubes are close and some are apart.

pages.text: Spheres This solid is a sphere. It has no flat faces, edges, or vertices.
pages.brief: A sphere is shown as a round solid with no flat faces, no edges and no vertices. Its surface curves smoothly all around. Nothing flat or pointed appears on the sphere. The sphere has only a curved surface.

pages.text: A sphere has a curved surface and nothing else. All points on a sphere’s curved surface are the same distance from the center.
pages.brief: A sphere is drawn with a smooth curved surface. Every point on the curved surface is the same distance from the center. No flat face, edge or vertex is shown. The surface curves evenly in every direction.

pages.text: Leara looks for spheres in the sports shop. She knows they have: • no faces, edges, or vertices • a curved surface • surfaces on which all points are the same distance from the center.
pages.brief: Leara searches a sports shop for spheres. Spheres are shown with no faces, edges or vertices and a curved surface. All points on each sphere’s surface are the same distance from its center. Leara looks among the sports shop objects.

pages.text: How many spheres can you see?
pages.brief: A group of spheres is arranged for readers to look at. The spheres are different sizes and positions. Each sphere has a smooth curved surface and no flat faces, edges or vertices. Some spheres are close and some are apart.

pages.text: Cylinders This solid is a cylinder. It has two faces. The faces are circles. No matter how hard you look, you will not find a single vertex on a cylinder. Cylinders also have curved surfaces.
pages.brief: A cylinder is shown with two flat circular faces and a curved surface. No vertex appears anywhere on the cylinder. The two circular faces are at opposite ends. The cylinder’s curved surface joins the two circular faces.

pages.text: Cones This solid is a cone. A cone has only one face that is a circle.
pages.brief: A cone is shown standing upright with one flat circular face visible. The rest of the cone curves around. The cone has only one face, and that face is shaped like a circle. No other flat face is shown.

pages.text: House and Neighborhood Ruben and Megan look for cylinders and cones around their house and neighborhood. They know cylinders have: • two faces shaped like a circle • no vertices • curved surfaces They know cones have: • one face shaped like a circle.
pages.brief: Ruben and Megan walk around their house and neighborhood looking for cylinders and cones. Nearby cylinders have two circular faces, no vertices and curved surfaces. Nearby cones have one circular face. The two look for these solids in the places around them.

pages.text: How many cylinders and cones do you see?
pages.brief: A collection of cylinders and cones is shown for readers to look at. Some stand upright and some lie on their sides. Each cylinder has two circular faces; each cone has one circular face. The solids appear in different sizes and positions.

pages.text: Square Pyramids This solid is a square pyramid. It has four faces that are shaped like triangles. They are connected by four edges. It also has a face that is shaped like a square. There is one vertex on top of a square pyramid.
pages.brief: A square pyramid is shown with four triangular faces connected by four edges. It also has a square face at the base. One vertex sits on top of the pyramid. The triangular faces meet the square base.

pages.text: When a square pyramid is turned over, you can see four more vertices on the bottom. There are five vertices in all, including the one on top. It is a square pyramid because the face on the base is square. There are four more edges that connect the triangular faces to the base. Square pyramids have eight edges in all.
pages.brief: A square pyramid is turned over so its square base is visible. Four vertices appear around the bottom, and with the top vertex there are five in all. Four more edges connect the triangular faces to the base, making eight edges.

pages.text: Around the World Here’s an amazing group of square pyramids! You would have to go to Giza, in Egypt, to find them.
pages.brief: A group of square pyramids is shown at Giza, in Egypt. The pyramids have triangular faces and square bases. They stand together as an amazing group of square pyramids. The group rises from the ground in Egypt.

pages.text: Solids really are all around. Ruben and his friends saw them in their neighborhood and across the world. Where can you find solids around you?
pages.brief: Ruben and his friends look around their neighborhood and across the world. Solid figures appear all around them. Ruben and his friends have seen solids in many places. They consider where solids can be found around them.

pages.text: Draw lines to match each shape to its name.
pages.brief: Several solid figures are arranged in a matching activity. A rectangular prism, cube, sphere, cylinder, cone and square pyramid appear. Each shape is set out to be matched with its name, and space is left for drawing connections.

books.title: What's Your Money Worth?
books.art_why: Real-world money, shoppers, and market scenes can be photographed.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with a Dollar Bill and a Dollar Coin Megan has a dollar coin. Tony has a dollar bill. A dollar coin and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Megan holds a dollar coin and Tony holds a dollar bill. The two children stand side by side, comparing the coin and the bill. The picture shows that a dollar coin and a dollar bill are each worth one dollar.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Fifty-Cent Coins Tony has two fifty-cent coins. Megan has a dollar bill. Two fifty-cent coins and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar. Making One Dollar with Quarters Megan has four quarters. Tony has a dollar bill. Four quarters and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Tony shows two fifty-cent coins while Megan shows a dollar bill. Then Megan shows four quarters while Tony shows a dollar bill. The children compare the coins and bill, showing both groups are worth one dollar.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Nickels Megan has a dollar bill. Tony has twenty nickels. Tony groups his nickels in pairs. He skip-counts to see how much money he has. By what number does he skip-count? A dollar bill and twenty nickels are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Megan holds a dollar bill while Tony shows twenty nickels. Tony groups the nickels in pairs and skip-counts them to see how much money he has. The children compare the nickels with Megan’s dollar bill, both worth one dollar.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Pennies Kaya has a dollar bill. Ruben has one hundred pennies. He groups them into ten stacks. Each stack has ten pennies. = One hundred pennies and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Kaya holds a dollar bill while Ruben shows one hundred pennies. Ruben groups the pennies into ten stacks, with ten pennies in each stack. The picture compares the stacks of pennies with Kaya’s dollar bill, both worth one dollar.

pages.text: Bills Greater Than One Dollar Rose works in the market. A shopper buys twenty-six dollars’ worth of food. He pays with five five-dollar bills and a one-dollar bill. Here’s how Rose groups the money to count it.
pages.brief: Rose works in a market. A shopper buys twenty-six dollars’ worth of food and pays with five five-dollar bills and one one-dollar bill. Rose stands at the counter and groups the bills to count the shopper’s money.

pages.text: Counting Bills and Coins The next shopper pays with bills and coins. Her total is three dollars and sixteen cents or $3.16. Rose first groups the bills and coins. She orders the coins from greatest value to least value.
pages.brief: The next shopper pays with bills and coins. Her total is three dollars and sixteen cents, or $3.16. Rose groups the bills and coins, ordering the coins from greatest value to least value so she can count the money.

pages.text: Money and Things Have Value Things such as food and clothing have a value. This means they are worth something. Money has value, too. It can be used to buy food and clothing. When people buy things, they are giving money for something of equal value. Work has value also. People are paid money for their work, or jobs. The owner of the market pays Rose money for doing her job.
pages.brief: Food and clothing are shown with value, meaning they are worth something. Money can be used to buy food and clothing. People give money for things of equal value, and work has value too. The market owner pays Rose money for doing her job.

pages.text: Kaya does a job for her Uncle Alton. She brushes his cat for two dollars. He uses a one-dollar bill and these coins to pay Kaya exactly two dollars.
pages.brief: Kaya does a job for her Uncle Alton, brushing his cat for two dollars. Uncle Alton uses a one-dollar bill and coins to pay Kaya exactly two dollars. Kaya works with the cat, and the payment is shown beside them.

pages.text: Ruben earns two dollars and seventy-five cents a week when he feeds Mrs. Lee’s dog. Mrs. Lee has these bills and coins shown below. How could Mrs. Lee count out the exact money to pay Ruben for one week’s work with the fewest coins?
pages.brief: Ruben earns two dollars and seventy-five cents a week feeding Mrs. Lee’s dog. Mrs. Lee has bills and coins. She needs to count out the exact money to pay Ruben for one week’s work with the fewest coins.

pages.text: Making Exact Amounts Ruben has earned eight dollars and twenty-five cents for a few weeks of work. He wants to buy a toy robot. Will he have enough money? $7.85.
pages.brief: Ruben has earned eight dollars and twenty-five cents for a few weeks of work. He wants to buy a toy robot priced at $7.85. He looks at the toy robot and his money, wondering whether he has enough.

pages.text: Ruben has the money shown below. He counts out the exact amount he will need. What does exact amount mean? How can Ruben count out the exact amount?
pages.brief: Ruben has the money shown. He counts out the exact amount he will need. The picture shows Ruben with his money as he counts, working out what exact amount means and how to count out the exact amount.

pages.text: Kesha wants to buy a pin for her mother. She has these dollar bills and coins. What is the value of the pin? Does Kesha have the exact amount that she needs to buy it?
pages.brief: Kesha wants to buy a pin for her mother. She has dollar bills and coins. The pin’s value is shown with the money. Kesha looks at the pin and her money, checking whether she has the exact amount she needs.

pages.text: Kesha uses this money to buy the pin. Is the money equal to, more than, or less than the value of the pin?
pages.brief: Kesha uses her money to buy the pin. She has the pin and her money on the counter. The picture asks whether her money is equal to, more than, or less than the value of the pin.

pages.text: Making Change Tanner also wants to buy a pin for his mother. He has these dollar bills. $2.84 What is the value, or price, of the pin? Does Tanner have the exact amount he needs to buy it?
pages.brief: Tanner wants to buy a pin for his mother. He has dollar bills. The pin’s price is $2.84. Tanner looks at his bills and the pin, checking whether he has the exact amount he needs to buy it.

pages.text: Tanner has more than the exact amount of money to buy the pin. He can buy it and get back money called change. How much change did Tanner get back? =.
pages.brief: Tanner has more than the exact amount of money to buy the pin. He buys the pin and gets back money called change. The picture shows Tanner with the pin and the change he got back.

pages.text: Ruben has a dollar bill. He uses it to buy a ball. How much change will Ruben get back? Count on from the cost of the ball until you get to one dollar. =.
pages.brief: Ruben has a dollar bill. He uses it to buy a ball. The picture shows Ruben with the ball and his dollar bill, counting on from the cost of the ball until he gets to one dollar to find his change.

pages.brief: Isaac buys a wind-up toy for $2.52. He wants as few coins as possible for his change. He uses his money for the toy. The picture shows Isaac with the wind-up toy and the money he uses.

pages.brief: Phoebe has bills and coins to buy some hair clips. She gets the hair clips and change. The picture shows Phoebe with the hair clips and the change, asking what coins or bills she used to pay.

pages.brief: Megan has a five-dollar bill. She needs two quarters for the vending machine. She asks Tony to exchange money with her. Tony has money, and Megan asks whether he can exchange some of it for her five-dollar bill and still have two quarters left for the machine.

pages.brief: Megan gives Tony her five-dollar bill. Tony gives Megan money equal to her five-dollar bill. The picture shows the exchange. It also shows whether Tony still has two quarters left to use in the machine.

pages.text: If you had three dollars, which item would you buy? Which bills or coins would you get back for change? Think about what you learned about what your money is worth. Toy Cars.
pages.brief: Toy cars are shown, and three dollars is available to spend. The picture asks which item would be bought and which bills or coins would come back as change, thinking about what money is worth.

books.title: Tornadoes
books.art_why: Tornadoes and storm damage are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction What can lift roofs from buildings and sweep houses into the air? Tornadoes can. Tornadoes come in many sizes. Some tornadoes are only a few feet (1 m) across. Others are more than a mile (2 km) wide. Some tornadoes touch down for a short time. Others travel for hundreds of miles.
pages.brief: A huge tornado touches down near a town, lifting the roof off a building while another smaller tornado spins nearby. A house is swept into the air. The scene shows tornadoes of different sizes, some short-lived and some traveling far across open land.

pages.text: How Tornadoes Form Why do tornadoes happen? Scientists are not sure. Tornadoes come from giant thunderstorms called supercells. A supercell happens when warm, moist air rises to mix with cold, dry air.
pages.brief: A giant supercell thunderstorm towers over flat land. Warm, moist air rises from the ground while cold, dry air moves in above it. The two air masses meet inside the huge dark cloud. Scientists watch, unsure exactly why tornadoes happen.

pages.text: The mixing of cold and warm air causes the air to spin. The spinning wind turns into a cloud in a funnel shape. As the cloud turns, the wind becomes stronger. When the funnel cloud touches the ground, it is a tornado.
pages.brief: Inside the storm, cold and warm air mix and the wind begins to spin. The spinning wind forms a funnel-shaped cloud hanging below the storm. The funnel cloud turns and strengthens. When it touches the ground, it becomes a tornado.

pages.text: Measuring Tornadoes Scientists have a way to measure the strength of tornadoes. They look at the harm caused by a tornado. They use the amount of harm to estimate the wind speed. They use a special scale called the EF Scale. The EF Scale measures the strength of the tornado.
pages.brief: Scientists walk past damaged buildings and fallen trees, studying the harm a tornado caused. They use that damage to estimate how fast the wind was blowing. One scientist holds a special scale used to measure tornado strength, the EF Scale.

pages.text: Where Tornadoes Form Tornadoes may be hard to measure, but scientists have a good idea where they’ll strike. It’s true that a tornado can hit anywhere in the world at any time. Most tornadoes happen in the central part of the United States. This area is called Tornado Alley. TORNADO ALLEY TORNADO ALLEY.
pages.brief: A wide view of the central United States shows the area where most tornadoes happen. A tornado touches down on open land within this region. The scene suggests that tornadoes can strike anywhere in the world, but this central area is called Tornado Alley.

pages.text: More than one thousand tornadoes strike Tornado Alley each year.
pages.brief: Many tornadoes spin across Tornado Alley at the same time. Funnels touch down over fields and towns, showing that more than one thousand tornadoes strike this area each year. The sky is dark and stormy above the wide central United States landscape.

pages.text: Tornado Safety There is no way to be sure that a tornado will strike. The National Weather Service (NWS) tries to help people stay safe during tornadoes. If they put out a tornado watch, a tornado might strike. If they put out a tornado warning, a tornado has been spotted.
pages.brief: People from the National Weather Service monitor storms and share safety information. One person points to a stormy sky while another listens. They explain that a tornado watch means a tornado might strike, while a tornado warning means a tornado has been spotted.

pages.text: If there is a tornado warning, it’s important to get to a safe place. Go indoors. The safest place is a basement. If you can’t get to a basement, go into a closet or bathroom. Stay away from windows.
pages.brief: People hurry indoors during a tornado warning. They go down into a basement, the safest place. Another person moves into a small closet or bathroom, staying away from windows. The building is shown with strong wind outside.

pages.text: The spinning air in a tornado makes things fly around. This can be dangerous. It’s always important to protect your head. You should get close to the ground. Go under a desk or table. You can even lie down in a bathtub.
pages.brief: Inside a tornado, spinning air lifts objects and sends them flying. A person crouches close to the ground under a desk, protecting their head with their arms. Another person lies down inside a bathtub. The scene shows how dangerous flying debris can be.

pages.text: If you are in a tall building, go to the stairs. If you are in a car, safely find lower ground and lie down. Otherwise, wear your seatbelt and lean forward. If you are outside, lie down on the ground. It isn’t safe to stay inside a mobile home in a tornado. It is better to go into a car or outside. Famous Tornadoes.
pages.brief: People in different places react to a tornado. In a tall building, a person heads for the stairs. In a car, someone finds lower ground and lies down, or wears a seatbelt and leans forward. Outside, a person lies on the ground. Near a mobile home, people move toward a car or outside.

pages.text: Conclusion Tornadoes are scary examples of the power of nature. People still have many questions about tornadoes. What causes a tornado? What is it really like inside a tornado? Maybe we will find out one day.
pages.brief: A powerful tornado moves across the land, showing the scary force of nature. People look at the storm and wonder about the questions that remain: what causes a tornado, and what is it really like inside one? They hope to find out one day.

books.title: Tokyo Imperial Palace
books.art_why: It covers Edo Castle, a 1657 fire, and 1800s construction that cannot be shown in real photos.

pages.text: A Peaceful Place The city of Tokyo is very busy and modern. The Imperial Palace sits in the middle of that city. It is a peaceful place. The emperor and empress of Japan live there.
pages.brief: The city of Tokyo is very busy and modern, and the Imperial Palace sits in the middle of that city as a peaceful place; the emperor and empress of Japan live there inside the palace.

pages.text: Where Is It? Tokyo is on the east coast of Japan. The Imperial Palace lies in the heart of Tokyo. It is near the Japanese National Theatre and Tokyo Disneyland.
pages.brief: Tokyo is on the east coast of Japan, and the Imperial Palace lies in the heart of Tokyo, near the Japanese National Theatre and Tokyo Disneyland; the palace is located within the busy city of Tokyo.

pages.text: History of the Palace A castle has stood on the site of the Imperial Palace for hundreds of years. In the early 1600s, a powerful lord built a grand castle called Edo Castle there. Sadly, its beautiful main tower burned down in 1657. Visitors can still see the stone base of that tower on the grounds of the Imperial Palace.
pages.brief: A powerful lord builds grand Edo Castle in the early 1600s; its beautiful main tower burns down in 1657, and visitors today can still see the stone base of that tower on the Imperial Palace grounds.

pages.text: In the 1800s, the emperor decided to move his home to the site of Edo Castle. He ordered workers to build a new palace there. They finished building the new Imperial Palace in 1888. The new palace looked Japanese on the outside. Inside, though, there were many European decorations and furniture.
pages.brief: In the 1800s, the emperor decides to move his home to the site of Edo Castle and orders workers to build a new palace finished in 1888; the outside looks Japanese, while the inside has European decorations and furniture.

pages.text: During World War II, the United States bombed the area around the palace. The palace was made of wood, so it was damaged by fires. After the war, Japan built the palace again. This time, workers used cement instead of wood. They finished in 1968. The building we can see today looks very much like it did before the war.
pages.brief: During World War II, the United States bombs the area around the palace, and fires damage the wooden palace; after the war Japan rebuilds it with cement instead of wood and finishes in 1968, looking much like before the war.

pages.text: Building the Walls The palace grounds have stone walls around them. Workers used a special way of building to make them. The builders stacked stones to form the walls. They did not use any mortar to keep the stones together. That way, all the rainwater could drain out through the cracks. Even heavy rain would not damage the walls. This way of building also helped protect the walls in an earthquake. Some of the stone walls from the early 1600s still stand today.
pages.brief: Workers stack stones to form stone walls around the palace grounds without using any mortar, so rainwater drains through the cracks; heavy rain does not damage the walls, the walls are protected in an earthquake, and some stone walls from the early 1600s still stand today.

pages.text: Four Sections The Imperial Palace in Tokyo has four areas. They are the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, Kitanomaru Park, the East Gardens, and the Imperial Palace inner grounds.
pages.brief: A view of the Imperial Palace site in Tokyo, which is made up of four areas: the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, Kitanomaru Park, the East Gardens, and the Imperial Palace inner grounds; these four areas together form the palace site.

pages.text: The Imperial Palace Outer Garden is a free park. The Nijubashi Bridge is a famous bridge in this area. The East Gardens are also open for people to visit. The East Gardens are beautiful all year. Some of the oldest buildings and walls in this area are from the 1600s.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace Outer Garden is a free park with the famous Nijubashi Bridge; the East Gardens are also open to visitors, beautiful all year, and some of the oldest buildings and walls there are from the 1600s.

pages.text: The emperor and empress live on the Imperial Palace grounds. The palace itself is also in this area of the site. The palace is a large building. It has two stories aboveground and one story below the ground. The emperor does his work for the government there. He takes part in special events. He throws big parties for important visitors.
pages.brief: The emperor and empress live on the Imperial Palace grounds, where the large palace building has two stories aboveground and one below; the emperor does government work there, takes part in special events, and throws big parties for important visitors.

pages.text: Natural Beauty The emperor protects nature at the Imperial Palace. More than 3,600 species of animals and insects live there. So do more than 1,300 species of plants. It is amazing to find so much natural beauty in such a big city.
pages.brief: The emperor protects nature at the Imperial Palace, where more than 3,600 species of animals and insects and more than 1,300 species of plants live; so much natural beauty is amazing to find in such a big city.

pages.text: An Important Landmark The Imperial Palace is important even today. Therefore, the government takes very good care of it. Many people exercise on the palace grounds. Many others visit the palace for fun. Every spring, one million visitors come to see the cherry trees bloom there. People enjoy the beauty and history of the Imperial Palace.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace is an important landmark today, and the government takes very good care of it; many people exercise on the palace grounds, many others visit for fun, and every spring one million visitors come to see the cherry trees bloom.

books.title: Animal Defenses
books.art_why: All the animals and defenses described exist in the real world today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction In the wild, many animals eat other animals. These predators are always on the hunt for their next meal. Their prey, however, don’t just sit around waiting to be eaten. These animals have developed many ways to defend themselves.
pages.brief: A wild predator moves low through tall grass, eyes fixed on the animals ahead. The grazing animals stand alert, heads up, ready to bolt or defend themselves. The scene spreads across open ground under a wide sky, showing hunters and the hunted sharing the same wild place.

pages.text: Claws, Teeth, Spikes Lions, tigers, and bears have sharp teeth and claws. Some smaller animals, like house cats and raccoons, also have them.
pages.brief: A lion bares long sharp teeth and shows heavy claws on a raised paw. Beside it, a tiger and a bear display their own teeth and claws. In the foreground a small house cat and a raccoon show the same sharp points on a much smaller scale.

pages.text: Some animals have sharp spikes to keep predators away. Porcupines are covered in sharp spikes called quills. The quills are made of the same stuff as human hair and fingernails. The quills can stick in predators’ skin like needles. Hedgehogs also have quills. When hedgehogs are attacked, they roll up in a ball so all their quills point out.
pages.brief: A porcupine stands in the open, its body covered in long sharp quills pointing in every direction. Nearby a hedgehog has rolled itself into a tight ball, quills sticking outward all around it, so nothing soft is left showing to a predator.

pages.text: Animals That Use Venom Some animals can hurt or even kill predators with a bite or a sting. These animals deliver venom to defend themselves.
pages.brief: A small animal shows bared fangs while another raises a stinger, both turned toward a much larger predator looming close. The scene shows a bite and a sting ready to deliver venom as a defense, in a wild setting of leaves and ground.

pages.text: Some snakes have venom. The venom in the bite of a king cobra is strong enough to kill an elephant! Bees, wasps, and some ants also have venom. All spiders have fangs, and most spiders have venom, too.
pages.brief: A king cobra lifts its head and spreads its hood, fangs showing. Around it, bees and wasps hover and ants crawl, and a spider displays its fangs. They share a leafy outdoor setting where each small creature carries venom of its own.

pages.text: Animals That Use Poison Some animals are poisonous. That means their bodies release a dangerous substance when another animal attacks or tries to eat them. The puffer fish has poison in its skin, and some puffer fish also have spikes to keep enemies away. The poison tastes bad to other fish, and it can be deadly.
pages.brief: A puffer fish floats inflated and round, spikes standing out from its skin, in blue water. A larger fish approaches with its mouth open, then turns away, as if the bad taste and the poison in the puffer fish's skin have driven it off.

pages.text: The golden poison frog is one of the most poisonous animals in the world. It is only about 5 centimeters (2 in.) long, but its skin is coated with a strong poison. Venom or Poison?
pages.brief: A tiny golden poison frog, only about five centimeters long, sits on a wet green leaf. Its bright yellow skin shines in the damp forest light. Nothing comes near it, because the frog's skin is coated with a strong poison that keeps predators away.

pages.text: Camouflage Some animals defend themselves by using camouflage, or blending in with the world around them. Some squid can change their skin color to hide in the water or to confuse predators. Some insects are the same color as the leaves or branches they live on. For example, the dead-leaf butterfly really looks like a dead leaf when its wings are closed.
pages.brief: A squid drifts in blue water, its skin shifting color as it blends into the water around it. On a branch, an insect matches the green leaves. A dead-leaf butterfly rests with wings closed, looking exactly like a dry brown leaf.

pages.text: Zebras are black with white stripes and travel in groups. Their predators have trouble seeing where one zebra ends and another one begins. This makes it more difficult for predators such as lions to hunt zebras.
pages.brief: Zebras stand close together in a herd, black and white stripes running into one another across their bodies. A lion watches from a distance, its eyes sweeping the group, unable to pick out where one zebra ends and the next begins.

pages.text: Other Defenses Most predators catch live prey, so some animals by playing dead. The opossum is famous for playing dead when it is afraid. If a hognose snake is attacked, it puffs up and hisses just like a cobra. If that fails, it rolls onto its back and releases a stinky liquid. When it does, it looks and smells dead.
pages.brief: An opossum lies on its side, limp and still, playing dead. A hognose snake puffs up and hisses with its head raised, then rolls onto its back and lets out a stinky liquid, lying there looking and smelling dead among the leaves.

pages.text: Some animals, like deer, defend themselves by being faster than the predators that hunt them. Other animals defend themselves by leaving body parts behind. Many lizards lose their tails when attacked. This distracts predators and makes it easier for the lizards to run quickly. Some lizards can even grow their tails back later!
pages.brief: A deer sprints across open ground, long legs stretched out, leaving a chasing predator behind. Nearby, a lizard breaks away and its tail stays behind on the ground, wriggling, while the lizard runs free toward cover.

pages.text: Conclusion Predators and prey are both necessary in the wild. Both add to the balance of the natural world. Different types of defenses give all animals a fighting chance.
pages.brief: A predator and its prey stand together in the same wide wild landscape, one watching, one grazing. Around them the natural world carries on, both animals part of the same balance, each with its own way of surviving.

books.title: The Baobab
books.art_why: The book includes an 1890 image, long-ago uses, and a legend, so drawings fit.

pages.text: An 1890 photo of an African baobab.
pages.brief: An African baobab tree as it appeared in 1890 stands in its landscape. Its thick trunk and spreading branches introduce the lands of Africa, the giants of the savanna, the baobab’s gifts, a different kind of tree house, dying giants, and a glossary.

pages.text: Where in the World Do Baobabs Grow? ASIA N PACIFIC Africa OCEAN INDIAN OCEAN Australia ATLANTIC Madagascar OCEAN Most baobab trees grow in Africa, Madagascar, and Australia. The Lands of Africa Africa has large, sandy deserts. It has thick, dark jungles. It also has open, grassy plains. The plains, known as the African savanna, are not just made up of grass,. They are called. These “trees of life” have helped the people and other animals of the savanna for thousands of years.
pages.brief: A view of the world shows Africa, Madagascar, and Australia, where most baobab trees grow. Nearby are Africa’s large sandy deserts, thick dark jungles, and open grassy plains called the savanna. These “trees of life” have helped people and animals for thousands of years.

pages.text: Giants of the Savanna Finding a baobab is easy trees rise high above the flat plains. A full-grown baobab can be 18 meters (59 ft.) tall. That’s taller than a five-story building! The Big Tree, a famous baobab in Limpopo, South Africa, is about 1,200 years old. The Baobab.
pages.brief: A tall, full-grown baobab rises high above a flat savanna plain. It stands taller than a five-story building. The Big Tree, a famous baobab in Limpopo, South Africa, is shown as an ancient tree about 1,200 years old.

pages.text: Elephants get water from baobab trunks during Africa’s dry season. Baobab trees have thick, barrel-. The oldest trees have trunks that are 9 meters (30 ft.) across. Like barrels, the trunks hold a lot of water. This is important because the savanna is a dry place. Being able to store water helps in the savanna. Baobabs also have strange branches. Their branches spread out like roots. When a baobab sheds its leaves, the tree looks as if it is upside down!
pages.brief: Elephants gather at a baobab during Africa’s dry season and get water from its trunk. The tree has a thick, barrel-shaped trunk holding water and strange branches spreading out like roots. With no leaves, it looks as if it is upside down.

pages.text: The Baobab’s Gifts The wildlife and people of the savanna get many things from the. The tree’s soft wood is filled with water. The leafy branches give cool shade from the hot Sun. A giraffe in Zambia, Africa, rests in the shade of a giant baobab. The Baobab.
pages.brief: A giraffe in Zambia, Africa, rests in the cool shade of a giant baobab. The tree’s leafy branches block the hot Sun, and its soft wood is filled with water. The wildlife and people of the savanna receive many gifts from it.

pages.text: Bats help spread pollen from one baobab flower to another. Bats drink sweet nectar from the tree’s white flowers. The flowers grow into fruit. The fruit bakes in the sun and dries. Its green coating turns into a hard shell. Then it is picked by hand.
pages.brief: Bats hover near white baobab flowers and drink sweet nectar, spreading pollen from one flower to another. The flowers grow into fruit that bakes in the Sun and dries. Its green coating becomes a hard shell before people pick it by hand.

pages.text: Baobab fruit is packed with. It has more vitamin C than an orange and as much calcium as milk! People use the fruit to make a healthy, tasty drink. It can also be used to make a kind of ice cream. Do You Know? Some people use baobab fruit and bark as medicine. A tea made from its bark is thought to cure stomachaches. The leaves may lower a fever. Oil from baobab seeds might help ease a toothache. Baobab fruit is also thought to help sore bones. The fruit of the baobab tree is sometimes called monkey bread. The Baobab.
pages.brief: Baobab fruit, sometimes called monkey bread, is shown with a healthy, tasty drink and a kind of ice cream made from it. The fruit has more vitamin C than an orange and as much calcium as milk. Bark, leaves, seeds, and fruit are used as medicine.

pages.text: A Different Kind of Tree House Baobab trees are useful in other. People weave long strings from the tree’s bark to make cloth, rope, and baskets. They use the roots to make red dye. A villager in Mali, Africa, weaves rope from the bark of a baobab tree.
pages.brief: A villager in Mali, Africa, weaves rope from long strings taken from a baobab tree’s bark. People use the bark to make cloth, rope, and baskets. They use the tree’s roots to make a red dye.

pages.text: A leopard and cub make their home inside a baobab tree in Botswana, Africa. The trees also give. Insects, lizards, monkeys, and other animals live in their branches and trunks. Long ago, people, too, used these trees as shelter. They did not make tree houses in their branches. They did not cut the wood to build houses. Instead, they lived inside a tree’s trunk! The Baobab.
pages.brief: A leopard and cub make their home inside a baobab tree in Botswana, Africa. Insects, lizards, monkeys, and other animals live in its branches and trunks. Long ago, people also used these trees as shelter and lived inside a tree’s trunk.

pages.text: A baobab was used as a bathroom long ago in Namibia, Africa. Baobab trunks have been used as homes and barns. People have found all sorts of uses for these trees!
pages.brief: A baobab tree in Namibia, Africa, is shown as it was used long ago as a bathroom. Baobab trunks have also been used as homes and barns, showing that people have found all sorts of uses for these trees.

pages.text: A baobab is hollow because it does not have a single trunk. Instead, it has several stems. The stems grow and attach to each other, forming a ring. Bark covers the stems and makes them look like one trunk. A baobab in Tanzania, Africa, is a main tourist attraction. The Baobab.
pages.brief: A baobab in Tanzania, Africa, is a main tourist attraction. The tree is hollow because it does not have a single trunk. Several stems grow and attach to each other in a ring, and bark covers them so they look like one trunk.

pages.text: Giant baobab trees have stood guard in Africa for centuries. Sadly, some of the oldest ones are dying off. At least nine trees that were thousands of years old have died since 2005. No one is sure why the trees are dying. Some people think the trees might have become sick over time. Other people worry that it is because Earth is getting warmer. Still others think it is just because the trees were old. Legend of the Baobab There are many stories about baobabs. One explains why the trees look so strange. According to the legend, the African god Thora had a baobab tree in his garden. He did not like how it looked, so he pulled it up and threw it over the garden wall. The poor baobab fell to Earth and landed upside down!
pages.brief: Giant baobab trees have stood in Africa for centuries, but some of the oldest are dying off. At least nine trees thousands of years old have died since 2005, and no one is sure why. In one legend, the god Thora threw a baobab over his garden wall, and it landed upside down on Earth.

pages.text: Without baobabs, life in Africa would not be the same. These giants of the savanna have so much to offer. Hopefully, people can look forward to their plentiful gifts for years to come. A famous baobab in Namibia, Africa, was used as a post office in 1940. Today, it is a national treasure. The Baobab.
pages.brief: A famous baobab in Namibia, Africa, was used as a post office in 1940 and is now a national treasure. Without baobabs, life in Africa would not be the same. These giants of the savanna have so much to offer, and people hope for their gifts for years to come.

pages.text: healthy and grow.
pages.brief: A baobab tree stands with an empty inside. Its main stems form the tree, and natural matter found in food helps living things stay healthy and grow. Around it, living things stay alive with protection from bad weather or danger.

books.title: Spiders
books.art_why: Spiders and their webs are real animals and natural things that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Do you jump when a spider crosses your path? Spiders may make some people nervous, yet they are mostly harmless to humans. More than forty thousand kinds of spiders live all over the world. They range in size from the head of a pin to a large dinner plate. The smallest may be lighter than a feather, while the heaviest can weigh as much as a softball.
pages.brief: A group of spiders of many sizes, from one as tiny as the head of a pin to one as large as a dinner plate, in a natural outdoor setting with grass, leaves, and soil. The smallest looks lighter than a feather; the heaviest looks as heavy as a softball.

pages.text: Traits Although spiders look like insects, they are different in many ways. Spiders have eight legs. Insects have only six. Spiders have two body parts including the head. Insects have three body parts including the head. Most spiders have eight eyes, and most insects have only two. Spiders do not have wings. Most insects do.
pages.brief: A spider with eight legs and two body parts, including its head, stands beside an insect with six legs and three body parts, including its head. The spider has eight eyes and no wings, while the insect has two eyes and wings. They are on a leaf outdoors.

pages.text: Life Cycle A female spider can lay thousands of eggs. After they hatch, the babies often stay near the mother until they can live on their own. Many spiders only live for a couple of years. Some, such as female tarantulas, can live up to thirty years.
pages.brief: A female spider rests beside a cluster of thousands of eggs in a sheltered outdoor spot. Newly hatched baby spiders stay close to the mother. Nearby, a female tarantula shows a spider that can live up to thirty years.

pages.text: Diet Spiders eat about half a billion tons of year. Without spiders, insects would destroy much of our food crops. Spiders also keep the number of pests such as mosquitos under control. Most spiders use their fangs to bite prey and inject venom—a poisonous liquid. Fangs work like a needle.
pages.brief: Spiders hunt insects in a garden or crop field. One spider bites its prey with fangs and injects venom, while other spiders keep mosquitoes and pests under control. Healthy food crops grow nearby, showing how spiders help protect the plants.

pages.text: Webs and Silk Some spiders make webs, which come in many beautiful shapes. These spiders use special body parts to make silk for their webs. The webs trap insects for them to eat. Many spiders add a sticky glue to the web. This makes it hard for insects to escape. Once an insect is caught, the spider wraps it tightly in silk.
pages.brief: Several spiders make webs of different beautiful shapes among plants. A spider uses special body parts to make silk for its web. An insect is trapped by sticky glue on a web, and the spider wraps it tightly in silk.

pages.text: Spider silk is stronger than steel. You can easily break a web because the threads are so thin. If the threads were as thick as a rope, the web would be strong enough to lift a jet airplane!
pages.brief: A spider web with very thin silk threads outdoors. Beside it, a thick rope made of spider silk is shown lifting a jet airplane, while the thin web can be broken easily because its threads are so thin.

pages.text: Some spiders also use their silk as a way to travel. Wind can blow the silk across a space, and it sticks to the other side. Spiders use the silk thread to walk from one twig or leaf to another.
pages.brief: A spider uses a silk thread as a bridge. Wind blows the silk across open space until it sticks to the other side, and the spider walks along the thread from one twig to another among leaves.

pages.text: Some baby spiders make a silk parachute to travel. The wind carries the piece of silk and lifts the spider with it. A parachute can carry a baby spider from just a short distance to over 100 kilometers (62 mi.).
pages.brief: A baby spider hangs from a silk parachute as wind lifts it through the air. The small spider can travel a short distance or more than 100 kilometers over land and sky, carried by the moving air.

pages.text: Some Cool Spiders Many spiders do not spin webs to catch prey. The spitting spider, for example, spits sticky liquid onto its prey. This liquid becomes hard and traps the insect, like a net. The jumping spider can jump from far away to surprise and attack its prey.
pages.brief: A spitting spider spits sticky liquid that hardens and traps an insect like a net. Nearby, a jumping spider leaps from far away to surprise and attack its prey. Both spiders are in a natural outdoor setting.

pages.text: The trapdoor spider digs a hole in the ground and covers it with silk. This spider springs up out of the trapdoor when an insect walks by. Tarantulas also spring out of holes in the ground to catch insects. Some tarantulas catch even bigger meals, such as birds and lizards.
pages.brief: A trapdoor spider at a silk-covered hole in the ground springs up as an insect walks by. Nearby, a tarantula springs from a hole to catch insects, and another tarantula catches a bird and a lizard.

pages.text: Spiders are unusual animals. They build beautiful webs, have powerful venom, and can sail through the air on silk. We depend on spiders to keep harmful insects under control. These skillful creatures have an important place in our natural world.
pages.brief: Spiders in a natural outdoor scene: one on a beautiful web, one with powerful venom, and one sailing through the air on silk. Harmful insects are kept under control near plants, showing spiders' important place in the natural world.

books.title: A Prairie Dog's Life
books.art_why: Keyword check selects drawing for this title.

pages.text: The Big Day Spring has come to the prairie. Today, Charlie will go outside for the first time. Charlie has lived his first few months below ground. Charlie is a black-tailed prairie dog. But is he really a dog? No! Prairie dogs are actually squirrels, part of the rodent family.
pages.brief: A young black-tailed prairie dog named Charlie sits inside a dark underground burrow, looking toward a bright tunnel opening. Spring sunlight touches the short prairie grass above. Charlie has spent his first months below ground, and today he will go outside for the first time.

pages.text: Pioneers named the prairie dog because they thought the animal’s call sounded like a dog’s bark. Charlie loves his warm, cozy burrow, but he wants to go outside. Lucky Charlie! Today his mother will take him and his three sisters above ground. They will learn about the big world outside.
pages.brief: Below ground, Charlie waits in a warm, cozy burrow with his mother and three sisters. His mother stands at the tunnel opening, ready to lead the pups above ground. Above them, a pioneer listens as a prairie dog’s call sounds like a bark. Charlie looks eager.

pages.text: Welcome to the Prairie The “prairie” part of Charlie’s name comes from his habitat. All of the world’s grasslands, or prairies, have burrowing mammals that create underground homes. In the United States, that animal is the prairie dog. When he is grown, Charlie will weigh 1.5 to 3 pounds (0.68-1.36 kg). Standing on his rear feet, he will be about 1 foot tall (30.48 cm). That is about the size of a large squirrel or a guinea pig.
pages.brief: On a wide prairie of short grass, Charlie stands on his rear feet, about one foot tall. He looks small beside a large squirrel and a guinea pig, showing his size. Around him stretches open grassland with burrow mounds in the distance. Sunlight shows his fur and small body.

pages.text: There are five types of prairie dog. They are the Gunnison’s, black- tailed, white-tailed, Mexican, and Utah prairie dogs. The black-tailed are the most common, living on lowland prairies.
pages.brief: Five kinds of prairie dog stand together on lowland prairie grass, with the black-tailed prairie dog nearest the front. The other four types stand behind, each slightly different in coat and build. Burrow mounds and flat grassland stretch behind them under a wide sky.

pages.text: Home Below Ground Charlie’s underground home is called a coterie (KOH-tur-ee). Each family has its own small coterie, a hole that is made up of small “rooms.” Many coteries together make a prairie dog colony. One colony can spread for hundreds of miles and house thousands of dogs!
pages.brief: A cutaway view of Charlie’s underground coterie shows a family burrow with several small rooms connected by tunnels. Around it, many similar coteries spread across the prairie, forming a huge colony. The colony reaches far into the distance, with thousands of prairie dog homes dotted through the grassland.

pages.text: Charlie and his sisters poke their noses outside their burrow. The sun is so bright compared to the dark underground. But it is wonderful! They climb out of their burrow and over the mound of dirt at its opening. All around them is short prairie grass and plants.
pages.brief: Charlie and his sisters poke their noses out of the burrow, blinking in bright sunlight after the dark underground. They climb over the mound of dirt at the opening. All around them grows short prairie grass and low plants, with open prairie stretching away under a sunny sky.

pages.text: Charlie’s Underground Home a) main mound b) listening post f ) ”nursery” for d) “dry room” g) second entrance Do You Know?
pages.brief: A cutaway view of Charlie’s underground home shows a main dirt mound above the burrow and a second entrance nearby. Inside are small rooms, including a nursery and a dry room, connected by tunnels. One tunnel rises to a listening post near the surface. Charlie stands within the dark burrow.

pages.text: Danger! Charlie and his sisters begin to explore. Before long, a prairie dog’s sharp bark cuts through the air. “Yee-ipp!” he shouts with a hop. He has spotted danger! “Yee-ipp!” Charlie’s father replies. All of the prairie dogs stand tall, alert. Even though there is danger, they stay. The dogs will stay very still and watch until the danger goes away.
pages.brief: Charlie and his sisters explore the prairie grass when a prairie dog barks a sharp warning and hops. Charlie’s father answers with the same call. All the prairie dogs stand tall and alert, very still, watching the distance. Charlie and his sisters stay close to the burrow mound, waiting as the danger remains.

pages.text: What might the danger be? Many predators hunt prairie dogs. Predators include coyotes, bobcats, prairie falcons, black-footed ferrets, and golden eagles.
pages.brief: Around the prairie, several predators watch the prairie dog colony: a coyote, a bobcat, a prairie falcon, a black-footed ferret, and a golden eagle. Each predator is shown in its hunting stance near grass, burrow mounds, or sky. The prairie dogs are small and wary in the distance, with the predators closing in from different directions.

pages.text: Perhaps the biggest danger of all is humans. Some people think prairie dogs destroy the land. These people try to harm prairie dogs by destroying their homes or killing them. Other people believe prairie dogs are important because their burrows bring air and water to the soil. Burrows also provide hiding places for other animals to escape predators.
pages.brief: Two groups of people stand on the prairie near prairie dog burrows. Some people look angry beside damaged burrow openings; others kneel and point to healthy soil and animals hiding in burrows. The prairie dogs watch from a distance. The scene shows both harm and protection around the colony.

pages.text: Summertime for Charlie Not all yips and barks signal danger. Some yips or barks signal a prairie dog is lonely or upset. Now Charlie hears more yips and barks from the older prairie dogs that signal it is safe. The threat is gone. Charlie and his sisters like playing outside in the sun. They will spend most of their summer outside.
pages.brief: Under warm summer sun, Charlie and his sisters play outside among short prairie grass. Older prairie dogs give soft yips and barks that signal safety. The threat is gone. Charlie runs and tumbles with his sisters near the burrow mound, and the whole colony relaxes in the sunshine.

pages.text: As summer turns to fall, they will prepare their burrow for winter. During winter, they will rarely go out into the harsh weather. Early next spring, the older females will have babies. And in late spring, Charlie will be an adult male. He will share in the watchdog duties. He will probably start a family and build his own coterie.
pages.brief: A seasonal scene shows Charlie and his family preparing their burrow as summer turns to fall, then staying inside during harsh winter. In early spring, older females have new babies. By late spring, Charlie is an adult male on watchdog duty, starting his own coterie.

books.title: Sound All Around
books.art_why: A modern science topic about sound, with real animals, instruments, ears and everyday objects that can all be photographed.

pages.text: What Makes Sound? Crash, boom, bam, bang, swoosh, and splash —sounds are all around us.
pages.brief: A vivid photo of everyday sounds bursting out at once — a splash of water flying up, and the sudden jolt of a crash, boom and bang as something heavy hits. The moment is loud and abrupt, filling the air with noise.

pages.text: People, animals, and objects make sounds. Even the weather makes sound. Sounds can be loud or soft. They can be pleasant or unpleasant.
pages.brief: A photo of three kinds of sound makers: a person calling out, an animal barking, and an object clattering down, with wind and rain making weather sound behind them. Some of it is loud, some soft, some pleasant, some not.

pages.text: Animals use sound in many ways. Humans use sound to communicate their thoughts and feelings. Other animals use sound to communicate, too. They use sound to defend themselves, attract a mate, or signal a warning.
pages.brief: A photo of animals using sound: a songbird calling from a branch to attract a mate, a deer lifting its head to warn the herd, and a dog standing tall and barking to defend its ground. Each one is communicating by sound.

pages.text: Humans have to make sounds. Drums, bagpipes, instruments make music. Horns, bells, and sirens sound warnings or call people to events. Alarm clocks that it is time to get out of bed.
pages.brief: A photo of people making sounds on purpose: a drummer beating a drum, a bagpiper blowing bagpipes and a band playing instruments to make music. A horn sounds, a bell rings, a siren wails a warning, and an alarm clock rings to wake someone.

pages.text: What Is Sound? Sound is made when an object vibrates, or moves back and forth very quickly. People make sound to talk when air vibrates vocal cords in their throats. Different vibrations in the vocal cords make different sounds.
pages.brief: A close photo of a person mid-sentence, mouth open, talking to someone. The view tightens on the throat, where air vibrates the vocal cords, and the cords are shown moving quickly back and forth, fast and slow, to make different sounds.

pages.text: Try This! Feel the Vibration • Get two rubber bands, one thick and one thin. • Stretch them over an open shoebox. • Pluck each rubber band. • Listen to the sounds they make. • How are the sounds different? Why?
pages.brief: A photo of two rubber bands, one thick and one thin, stretched over the open top of a shoebox on a table. A hand plucks the thin band, then the thick one, and each quivers as it sounds.

pages.text: A vibrating object makes the air around it move. This is how sound travels. It moves outward in all directions. For example, when a tree crashes to the ground, the air around it vibrates. When the vibrating air reaches your ear, you hear the sound of a crashing tree. The vibrating air is called sound waves. Sound waves also travel through solids and liquids.
pages.brief: A photo of a big tree crashing down in a forest and hitting the ground hard. The air around the trunk shimmers and pushes outward in every direction, travelling as sound waves, and the waves move through the soil and through water too.

pages.text: Different Sounds Not all sound is alike. Some sounds are loud. Others are quiet. The loudness of sound is called volume. The more air that vibrates, the louder the volume. For example, a lion’s roar vibrates more air than a buzzing bee’s wings. Sound also can be high or low. This is called pitch. Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates. Sirens vibrate quickly and have a high pitch. Bass drums vibrate slowly and have a low pitch.
pages.brief: A photo comparing loud and quiet, high and low: a lion with its mouth wide open, roaring and shaking lots of air, beside a tiny bee whose wings buzz softly. A siren screams high while a bass drum booms low and slow.

pages.text: Math Minute 1.
pages.brief: A quiet photo for a quick math minute: a boy sits at a table with his fingers raised, counting carefully and thinking hard as he works through a short set of number questions, his pencil resting on his notebook.

pages.text: Ears and Sound The outside of your ear is shaped to collect sound waves. The sound waves move from outside the ear to inside the ear. Tiny bones inside vibrate when they are struck by sound waves. The vibrating bones send messages through nerves to your brain. Your brain then interprets the messages as noise, music, talking, or other sounds.
pages.brief: A close photo of a human ear. The cupped outer ear collects sound waves, which travel inside to the eardrum and the tiny bones, and those vibrating bones send messages along nerves to the brain, which reads them as noise, music or talking.

pages.text: The inner parts of the ear are very sensitive. Very loud sounds can hurt your ears. Be careful around loud noises. Cover your ears with your hands, or wear coverings on your ears such as earphones or earplugs. Or simply move away from the loud sounds.
pages.brief: A photo of a child standing near a very loud speaker with both hands pressed firmly over their ears. Another person wears earplugs and earphones to block the noise, and a third walks away from the loud sound to a quieter spot.

pages.text: Conclusion We are surrounded by sounds. Vibrations make loud, quiet, high, and low sounds. Our ears pick up and our brain tells us what they are. Enjoy the of the world and be careful with your ears!
pages.brief: A photo of a world full of sound: a dog barking, a bird singing, a person talking, a car horn honking and music playing, all around a listening child who stands still and takes in the loud, quiet, high and low sounds.

books.title: Louis Braille: A Man and His Method
books.art_why: Louis Braille is a named historical person, so a cartoon treatment fits the biography.

pages.text: The Accident In 1809, Louis Braille was born in a small town in the country of France. One day at the age of three, Louis hurt himself. While playing in his father’s shoe workshop, he tried to make his own pair of shoes.
pages.brief: In a small town in France, baby Louis is born to his family. As a three-year-old boy, he plays in his father's shoe workshop, bending over leather and tools while trying to make his own pair of shoes.

pages.text: Louis picked up his father’s sharp awl and bent over. The awl went into Louis’s eye. His hurt eye became sick. Before long, the sickness spread to his other eye. By age five, Louis could no longer see. He was blind.
pages.brief: Young Louis bends over in the shoe workshop, holding his father's sharp awl; the tool goes into his eye. His hurt eye becomes sick, and the sickness spreads to his other eye, leaving the five-year-old boy blind.

pages.text: Louis went to school with children who could see. He learned by listening, but since he could not see, he could not read or write. Like many other parents of children who were blind back then, Louis’s parents feared for his future. However, when Louis was ten, they were able to send him to a special school in Paris.
pages.brief: Louis sits in a classroom with children who can see, listening carefully because he cannot read or write. At home, his parents look worried about his future. At ten, Louis travels to a special school for children who are blind in Paris.

pages.text: A New Sort of School The school in Paris was for boys who were blind. It was one of the first such schools in the world. Louis learned many skills at this school. He learned how to weave branches together to make chairs. He learned how to sew leather to make slippers.
pages.brief: At the Paris school for boys who are blind, Louis learns practical skills. He weaves branches together to make a chair and sews leather to make slippers, working with other blind boys in one of the first such schools in the world.

pages.text: Louis also learned how to read. He felt raised letters on a sheet of paper. The paper was pressed against copper wires shaped like letters. This made raised letters on the paper that fingers could feel. But the letters were difficult to read. Too many letters had similar shapes and felt the same. And the wire used to make these letters had to be shaped by people who could see. It seemed there had to be a better way for people who were blind to read.
pages.brief: Louis feels raised letters on a sheet of paper, learning to read by touch. The letters were pressed against copper wires shaped like letters, but many feel alike and are hard to tell apart. People who can see must shape the wires.

pages.text: Night Writing Charles Barbier, a soldier, invented a form of night writing for France’s army. Soldiers often hid in the dark. They did not want to use a light because they did not want to be found. Night writing used twelve small raised dots to form each letter. It gave soldiers a way to read in the dark. It also allowed soldiers to send messages to one another without using light or making a noise. This code was too hard for most soldiers to learn, however. The army decided not to use it, so in 1821, Barbier took the system to Louis’s school.
pages.brief: Soldier Charles Barbier shows night writing: groups of twelve raised dots that soldiers can feel in darkness without using a light or making noise. In 1821, Barbier brings this dot system to Louis's school, where Louis examines the raised dots.

pages.text: Louis believed a system of raised dots could be used to help people who are blind to read. He had been trying to create a touch system of his own for reading and writing. When he tried night writing, he knew it was the right idea but was also too difficult.
pages.brief: Louis sits with raised-dot samples at school, thinking about a touch system for reading and writing. He has been trying to create his own. Night writing gives him the right idea, but he sees that it is still too difficult.

pages.text: The night-writing system did not allow a fingertip to touch a whole letter. Readers had to move their finger to feel the whole symbol. Night writing also did not include periods, question marks, music signs, or numbers. Louis asked Barbier to change his system to make it easier, but the soldier would not change it.
pages.brief: Louis moves a fingertip across a long twelve-dot symbol, unable to feel the whole letter at once. He notices that night writing has no periods, question marks, music signs, or numbers. Louis asks soldier Charles Barbier to make the system easier, but Barbier refuses to change it.

pages.text: Louis’s Own System Over a few years, Louis made a shorter, easier form of this touch system. He used six dots instead of twelve to form each letter. It allowed a person’s fingertip to feel the entire symbol without having to move. This difference let people who are blind read much more quickly and easily.
pages.brief: Louis works at a table with small six-dot cells, designing a shorter, easier touch system. A person's fingertip can feel one whole symbol without moving. This change lets people who are blind read much more quickly and easily than with night writing.

pages.text: At age fifteen, Louis shared this new system with his classmates and the school. Several years later, Louis added similar dot codes for music and math. Today, we call this form of written language braille. It is named after Louis Braille, who helped invent it. Now, people who are blind use a stylus and a slate to write braille. Dots are punched on the back of heavy paper with a stylus. A slate is used to keep the dots spaced correctly. Sentences are written from right to left. Then the paper is flipped over, and the sentences are read from left to right.
pages.brief: At fifteen, Louis shows his six-dot system to classmates and the school. Years later he adds dot codes for music and math. A person who is blind uses a stylus and slate to punch dots into heavy paper from right to left; then the paper is flipped to read left to right.

pages.text: Braille can also be written using a Perkins Brailler, a typewriter-like machine. Braille gives people who are blind a way to both read and write. From Stylus to Smartphone.
pages.brief: A person who is blind sits at a Perkins Brailler, a typewriter-like machine, and presses keys to make raised braille dots. Beside the machine, a stylus, slate, and smartphone show how braille writing has moved from hand tools to modern devices.

pages.text: A Loved Teacher Braille became a teacher at the school he attended as a child. He was loved by his students. He died in 1852, but his form of writing lives on. Even though Louis Braille became blind at a young age, he never gave up. Instead, he overcame great obstacles, which made it possible for people who are blind to read.
pages.brief: Adult Louis Braille teaches at the Paris school he once attended, surrounded by students who respect and love him. Years after his death in 1852, people who are blind still read and write using the system he created, because he never gave up.
